blocks.alt: Watercolor view of two distant young dragons leaving luminous trails through a forming primordial cosmos.

blocks.text: The egg floated in the void.
There was no sky around it. No ground beneath it. No distant light by which it might have been seen.
It simply drifted, enormous and alone, through a darkness without edge or end.
They had no words. There were no places to remember, no voices to recall, no world beyond the curve of the shell.
If they dreamed at all, perhaps they dreamed only of warmth, of closeness, of the other presence curled beside their own.
A thin crack opened across the egg.
For the first time, the void knew what it was to be broken by sound.
And through that narrow crack came light.
A pale glow slipped through first, soft and pearlescent. Beside it came a darker radiance, black at its heart but alive with violet, blue, green, and colors that had never needed names.
A pale claw pressed through the shell. Almost at once, a dark claw broke through somewhere opposite it.
The quiet ended in a rush of sharp, bright sounds as pieces of shell broke free and tumbled into the darkness.
Two young dragons emerged among the drifting fragments.
One was pearlescent white, glowing softly from somewhere beneath his scales. Rose, silver, blue, and gold moved through that light when he turned.

His brother was dark, but not like the emptiness around them. His scales shimmered like raw oil, black at first glance and then suddenly violet, green, blue, or something stranger. A dim iridescent glow lived beneath them, as though darkness itself had learned how to shine.
For a while, neither did anything.
They drifted among the remains of the shell, still curled close by instinct.
The pale one saw the dark one.
The dark one saw the pale one.
Before either had known waking, the other had already been there.
The pale brother lifted a claw and touched the other's snout.
The dark brother blinked, then leaned into the touch.
They had no word for brother.
They had no word for love.
When one moved, the other followed. When one drifted too far, the other reached for him.
The void held nothing else, and for a time they wanted nothing else.
The pale brother pushed away from a piece of shell and shot into the darkness.
Behind him, a thin ribbon of pearly light remained.
The dark brother saw it too.
His own trail followed him: dimmer, deeper, shimmering violet and blue against the black.
Soon they were racing through the void, circling one another, diving through each other's glowing paths and turning sharply just to see what new shape their movement would leave behind.
Where they passed once, light lingered.
Where they passed again and again, it gathered.
Fine trails became broad veils. Curves crossed curves. Tiny points burned brighter where their paths met.
The brothers noticed only that the darkness was becoming prettier to play in.
They had no word for sky.
They had no word for star.
For now there was only their game, and the light it left behind.
Then the pale brother struck a drifting piece of shell with his tail.
The dark brother chased it, caught it between his claws, and threw it back.
The fragment sailed past the pale brother's head.
That was enough to begin another game.

They chased pieces of shell through the growing light. They struck them with claws, noses, wings, and tails. They collided with one another often enough that even surprise became part of the fun. When one sent a fragment too far, both raced after it. When one discovered a new way to make a piece spin, the other immediately tried to do it better.
There was no purpose in any of it.
They were awake. They were together. They were having fun.
During one collision, something small came loose from the pale brother's side.
He turned it over between his claws, fascinated by the soft glow still living inside it, then flicked it toward his brother.
The pale brother caught it and tossed it back.
Neither noticed the fine dust of eggshell clinging to its edge.
A tiny splinter struck the scale and stayed.
The dark brother batted it away too hard. It struck a larger fragment of shell, broke a piece loose, and carried that piece with it.
The pale brother crashed into him before he could stop.
When they separated, a dark iridescent scale drifted free from the second brother and struck the little mass between them.
The object now carried both of their light.
That made it immediately more interesting.
The pale brother snatched it first.
The dark brother lunged after him.
They tossed it back and forth, faster now. Each catch sent it spinning. Each throw pressed shell, dust, and scales more tightly together. Each collision drew in another tiny fragment.
At first it was only warm.
Sharp edges softened. Loose fragments sank into one another. The uneven clump rounded as it turned, gathering more of the broken egg around itself.
Soon neither brother could catch it in one claw.
They pushed it instead, striking it from opposite sides and racing after it whenever it escaped them.
The sphere grew hotter and brighter until even their own trails of light curled around its glow.
Still they did not understand what was happening.
They only knew that their toy kept changing.
Eventually it became too large to throw at all.
The pale one pressed a claw to its surface.
The dark one did the same from the other side.
Beneath them, shell and scale had become something neither had seen before.

Its outer fire slowly dimmed. Its surface folded as it cooled. Ridges rose. Hollows opened. Dark seams crossed pale stone. Deep within, pieces of both brothers remained fused with the remnants of the egg.
The twins watched for a while.
Then something else caught their attention, and they raced away together.
They did not know that they had made a world.
They did not know that the light behind them had become the first heavens, or that bright points now burned where their paths had crossed.
They did not know that, long after the young sphere cooled, the places where their scales lay buried would not remain empty forever.
Life would begin without either brother ever deciding that it should.
The sphere turning behind them was the first shard.
And it would not be the last.

blocks.alt: Watercolor view of an open rural village, its road, working buildings, fields, and the Old Forest.

blocks.text: Much later, beneath a sky born from light neither brother had ever intended to leave behind, a hammer struck glowing iron.
The sound rang through a small roadside village.

It was a close-built scatter of timber and stone around the road and the well. Fenced gardens and animal pens filled the spaces between homes, sheds, and barns. Beyond the last roofs, fields spread toward low hills, while the old woods stood as a darker line on the far side of the village.
The morning was mild and clear. Sunlight caught on damp grass beyond the road, and thin chimney smoke climbed almost straight in the still air.
Eight-year-old Calist Griffith looked up from the floor of his father's smithy.
He had been sweeping metal filings into a small pile near the open doorway, though most of his attention had long since wandered outside.
The village was small enough that Calist knew every roof and most of the hands that had repaired them.
To the wider world, the road beside it mattered more.

The road ran on toward a small fort that watched the border. It was one of the routes that kept the fort and the settlements around it connected to the interior. Merchants and supply wagons hauled food, lamp oil, salt, metal, leather, and other necessities toward the border. Soldiers came and went in small groups. Messengers carried orders outward and reports back inland.
And almost always, they brought stories.

His father, Alden Griffith, brought the hammer down again. Brown hair clung damply at his temples from the forge heat, and the sleeves of his work shirt were rolled above forearms marked by years of sparks.
Outside, hoofbeats approached along the road.
Three riders came into view beyond the open doors.
Calist knew the first one immediately.

Corvin Hale had visited often enough that Calist no longer thought of him as a stranger. He still wore the same sort of plain military coat and travel-stained boots as the soldiers who sometimes accompanied him, but he was older than most of them. Not old like the village elders, but old enough that grey showed at his temples and lines gathered around his eyes whenever he smiled.
Alden looked up from the anvil, hazel eyes already amused.
Corvin swung down from the saddle.
"Only the shoe. The horse has more sense than I do."
Calist grinned before remembering he was supposed to be sweeping.
"Finish the doorway. Then bring the hoof stand."
Calist immediately put the broom back to work.

The riders led their horses into the shade beside the smithy. One had a loose shoe. Another had a buckle on his sword belt that had nearly torn free. The third carried a dented piece of armor beneath one arm and set it carefully on the workbench.
Nothing about any of it looked like the stories Calist and the other village boys acted out.
There were no banners. No polished armor. No heroic procession.
There was mud on the soldiers' boots, dust in the folds of their clothes, sweat dried into the straps of their gear, and a smell of horse that reached the smithy before the horses did.
Not because they brought violence with them. What fascinated him was that they had been somewhere else.

Every stain on a coat came from a road he had never walked. Every dent had happened beyond the fields he knew. Every unfamiliar coin, strange bit of cloth, new turn of phrase, or half-finished complaint suggested that the world continued far beyond the village even when Calist could not see it.
He carried over the hoof stand while Alden crouched beside Corvin's horse.
Calist took the reins with both hands.
The horse barely seemed to notice him.
Alden lifted the hoof, inspected the worn shoe, and clicked his tongue.
"How long did you ride on this?"
Alden removed the bent nails one by one.
While he worked, the soldiers talked.

At first it was about the road. A bridge farther north had lost part of its railing. A wagon had broken an axle near the river bend. Rain had turned one of the smaller tracks into mud deep enough to swallow a boot.

One rider complained about a town where the innkeeper had charged him twice for the same meal. Another described a market so crowded that he had lost sight of his own horse while still holding its reins.

Corvin told them about a river crossing where the ferry had stopped halfway because a rope had come loose, leaving everyone drifting slowly downstream while the ferryman shouted instructions no one could hear.
Calist forgot to breathe for a moment.
Calist was slightly disappointed by that.
Alden continued working on the hoof.
"If you answer that, he'll keep you here until dark."
Later, one of the younger soldiers mentioned goblins they had seen near the road.
Calist's hands tightened around the reins.
"Four of them," the man said. "Maybe five. Hard to count when they're running."
"You said there were eight yesterday," Corvin replied.
"I said there might have been eight."
The younger soldier smiled at him.
"They saw him," Corvin said, pointing at the younger man, "and decided there were easier meals somewhere else."
By the time the story was finished, the encounter seemed to involve less glorious combat than wet boots, shouting, two lost arrows, and one soldier falling into a ditch.
That did not disappoint Calist as much as the younger man seemed to expect.
He wanted to know about the ditch too.
Where had the road been? How far from the village? Were there hills there? What kind of trees grew beside it? Had they seen any ruins? Had they passed other settlements?
"Alden, your son asks more questions than an officer."
Alden fitted the new shoe and set the hoof down.
"There. Try not to ruin this one before your next visit."
Calist's attention had already shifted to the sword at his hip.
Alden picked up the damaged buckle.
"He's interested in anything that keeps him from sweeping."
Alden looked at the thin line of filings still glittering near the wall.
Corvin did not draw his sword.
Instead he took the broom from Calist's hands.
"With a broom, unless your father has decided to start giving children steel."
Calist wrapped both hands around the broom handle and lifted it the way he had seen soldiers hold weapons in stories acted out by the village boys.
Corvin pushed him lightly on one shoulder.
Corvin handed the broom back without mocking him.
He moved Calist's front foot a little farther forward with the side of his boot.
"Now if someone pushes you, don't fight the push with your shoulders. Keep your weight under you."
This time Calist only rocked backward.
His father was already repairing the buckle.
"He can conquer the border after he finishes the floor."
Before he could put the broom back to the floor, running footsteps sounded outside.

Tarin reached the doorway first, his dirty-blond hair disordered from the run. Joric, bright blond even in the forge's shadow, nearly ran into him from behind. Eryn and Nalia were only a few steps back, Eryn's black hair and Nalia's red catching the forge light as they came.
Corvin looked around at the four new faces.

In a village this small, three soldiers and their horses outside the smithy were enough to pull curious children from nearby chores, especially when one of them was Corvin. Calist was not the only one who wanted stories from beyond the village.

Joric wanted to hear about the goblins. Tarin asked about the river. Eryn paid more attention to the bows and road gear than the swords. Nalia wanted to know whether the dented piece of armor had happened in a fight.
Calist watched them crowd around and felt slightly less foolish about all his own questions.
Alden let it continue for a minute.
Then he pointed toward the doorway with the damaged buckle.
"Whatever work you abandoned to get here still exists."
The children scattered slowly, each trying to get one last answer before going.
For the rest of the afternoon, Calist swept with his feet placed exactly the way Corvin had shown him.
Most days in the smithy were not like that.
Most days there were no soldiers.
The rush to see Corvin was unusual. The children themselves were not.

They came through the smithy all the time with small tasks adults had entrusted to them. Tarin brought kitchen knives that needed sharpening. Joric was sent to help hold a wheel steady while Alden checked a fitting. Eryn carried Garran's knives over to be sharpened and took them home again. Nalia delivered shears, bent pins, and other small pieces that needed repair, usually with strict instructions not to lose anything on the way.

Alden treated whichever child happened to be there much the same way he treated Calist. He kept them away from flying scale and hot iron, corrected them when they handled something badly, and found a safe job for idle hands if they stayed long enough.

Calist received the same treatment elsewhere. Tessa had fed him when Mara was occupied with someone sick. Garran had put leather in his hands and shown him how to hold it while he cut. Farmers had taught him where to stand around frightened animals and how to stack hay so it did not collapse the first time someone leaned against it.
No one called any of this teaching.
It was simply what happened when children grew up surrounded by adults who knew things the children did not yet know.
And the children were expected to help while they learned.
There were kitchen knives that had gone dull, shears with loose pins, cracked hinges, bent hooks, worn shovel heads, broken handles, plough fittings, wagon hardware, and horseshoes.

Calist learned their shapes before he learned why some horses needed one kind and others another. He learned where Alden kept nails of different sizes, which tongs were safe for him to carry, how far to stand from flying scale, when the water bucket needed filling, and how to tell from his father's voice whether "bring me the small hammer" meant now or immediately.
He liked the heat in winter. He liked the rhythm of the hammer. He liked watching a useless bent thing become useful again beneath Alden's hands.
The work was necessary. It was honest. It also changed very little.
The same farmers came with the same tools. The same wagons lost the same fittings. Horses threw shoes. Knives dulled. Hinges bent. Alden repaired them, and sooner or later they returned.
Calist understood why people valued that life. He valued it too.
But when soldiers rode into the yard, the day became different.
He simply did not stare at a repaired hinge the way he stared at a sword, or remember the story of a ploughshare the way he remembered a river he had never seen.
Whenever soldiers stopped, Calist found reasons to remain nearby.
He carried water before anyone asked.
He fetched tools that did not need fetching.
He swept the same patch of floor twice.

Soldiers complained about rain, bad food, commanders who changed their minds, boots that leaked, horses that bit, roads that vanished beneath mud, and the astonishing number of ways a buckle could break at the least convenient moment.

They spoke about other villages and crowded towns. Rivers broad enough that distant buildings looked small. Markets that filled whole streets. Hills where the grass changed color in autumn. Roads that continued for days beyond anything Calist knew.
Those were the stories he remembered at night.
Violence was part of their lives, and Calist listened when they spoke of it. But blood was never the part he carried to bed with him.
He remembered the idea that a person could leave one horizon behind and eventually find another.
Corvin returned several times each year, sometimes alone and sometimes with other soldiers.
Calist eventually learned, mostly by listening when adults thought he was busy elsewhere, that Corvin had once served beside Alden during the war.
That fact fascinated him almost as much as Corvin's sword.
Alden almost never spoke about the war.
When Calist asked what battles he had fought in, his father answered with things like, "Too many," or, "None worth remembering."
When Calist once asked whether he had killed anyone, Alden went silent long enough that Calist never asked again.
But when a soldier brought in torn mail, Alden's hands knew exactly how the rings should sit.
When a sword had been mistreated, he could often say how before its owner admitted it.
And in a wooden chest at home lay a plain shirt of chainmail, wrapped in cloth and kept cleaner than many things that were used every day.
Calist had seen Alden take it out more than once.
A weak ring was replaced. A spot of rust was cleaned away. Leather was oiled before it dried and cracked.
Then the armor went back into the chest.
To Calist, it was a relic from a life of stories.
To Alden, it seemed to be another thing that had been made well and therefore deserved not to be ruined.

blocks.text: Calist was ten when he made his first sword. It was terrible.
He knew that even before he finished it.

The blade was a length of scrap wood he had found behind the smithy. It was slightly crooked, too thick near the point, and thin where it should probably have been thick. The crossguard was another smaller piece of wood that he had forced through a rough slot with more determination than skill.
The grip was simply the part he had not cut away.
Calist held it out at arm's length and narrowed his eyes.
From far enough away, it looked like a sword.
Alden came around the side of the smithy carrying a bundle of iron rod.
Calist slowly lowered the wooden weapon.
Calist waited for him to say he had wasted the wood.
Instead Alden set down the iron rods, took the wooden sword, and ran one thumb along the grip.
"Sand this part. And round the edges here."
He tapped the grip and then the end of the crossguard.
"If you're going to hit your friends with it, at least try not to open their heads."
Alden gave him a strange look.
By evening, the grip was smoother.
By the next afternoon, Tarin and Joric had found sticks of their own.
The battle lasted nearly an hour.
No one agreed on who had won.
Calist insisted that getting struck after you were already "dead" did not count.
Tarin insisted that Calist had never said he was dead.
Joric declared himself a knight and therefore immune to being hit in the legs.
They argued until they forgot what they were arguing about and started again.
Calist tried to stand the way Corvin had shown him.
The stance did not make him a swordsman.
It did, however, make it harder for Tarin to knock him over.
That was enough to make him very proud of himself.
When Tarin and Joric finally ran home for supper, Calist followed not long afterward with the wooden sword across one shoulder.
The old woods waited beyond the far side of the village, as they always had.
The next morning, fog lay low over the fields.

It softened fences and swallowed the lower parts of distant trees. Roofs and chimney smoke faded into pale grey beyond a few dozen paces. The village was awake—Calist could hear a bucket at the well, a cart wheel complaining near the road, and Alden's hammer from the smithy—but the mist made every sound seem farther away.
Calist had a little time before Alden expected him at the forge. He took the wooden sword to the edge of the field to practice Corvin's stance again.
Instead, he found himself looking toward the woods.
He had seen them every day of his life.
There was nothing unusual to see.

Dark trunks rising through the fog beneath a thick canopy. Old paths used by hunters. Brambles along the edges, their leaves wet with beads of mist. A few places where children were told not to wander because the ground became steep or the undergrowth too dense.
He did not decide to go into the woods.
The wet grass brushed against his boots.
Then came the narrow strip beyond it.
Then the first line of trees.

The air changed beneath the branches. It was cooler there, carrying the smell of damp earth, wet leaves, and old bark. Fog drifted between the trunks in thin pale bands and hid the deeper woods a little at a time.
Behind him, the village sounds softened.
Ahead, there was only the woods.
He tightened his grip on the wooden sword.
He had no reason to be there. No game. No chore. No one to meet.
Still, going back immediately felt wrong in a way he could not explain.
So he walked a little farther.
Past a fallen tree silvered with age and slick with moisture.
Past a patch of ferns almost as tall as he was.
Past a narrow animal trail that disappeared between two ancient trunks and into the fog.
Something about that direction felt different.
Just a pull so quiet that if he had tried to explain it, he would have had nothing to say.
No knight emerged from behind the trees. No hidden ruin appeared. No monster waited in the mist.
Calist stood there until the fog between the trunks had begun to thin and another distant strike of Alden's hammer reminded him that he was supposed to be somewhere else.

Mara Griffith was waiting for him near the house with her arms folded. She had tied her black hair back for the morning's work, and her dark eyes moved from the damp hems of his clothes to the pale woods behind him.
Calist looked back toward the trees.
Mara stared at him for a moment, then sighed.
"Next time, tell someone before you disappear."
The next time still came without him planning it.
Sometimes months passed between those walks. Sometimes only weeks.
Calist never found anything waiting for him beneath the old trees.
But every so often, while carrying water to the forge or sweeping filings from the floor, he would look toward the woods and feel the same quiet pull.
As though he had forgotten something there.
By fourteen, Calist had changed in ways he usually noticed only after they had already happened.
At some point, the broom that had once reached almost to his chin became simply a broom.
At some point, Alden stopped moving the heavier buckets out of his reach and started saying, "Bring that here."

Calist's hands broadened. His shoulders began to fill out. The small burns on his forearms became older marks beside newer ones, and the work that had once required both hands and all his concentration slowly became ordinary.

The same road still cut past the same fields. The same roofs caught the morning light. The smithy still woke to the sound of Alden's hammer, animals still had to be fed whether it rained or not, and firewood somehow always needed carrying from one place to another.
Calist had once thought every household had its own work.
By the time he was old enough to be trusted with more of it, he understood that this was only partly true.
Everyone had things they did best.
That did not mean anyone did only those things.
When one of the older farmers slipped from a wet cart and hurt his ankle badly enough that Mara ordered him to stay off it, no meeting was called. No one stood in the road and assigned duties.
Alden repaired the broken cart shaft that afternoon instead of waiting for it to be brought to the smithy. Mara carried a bundle of herbs to the injured man's house. Someone else checked his fields.
And before breakfast was properly finished the next morning, Calist, Tarin Vale, Joric Fenner, Eryn Venn, and Nalia Reed had been sent to deal with the animals.
Joric stared into the goat pen.
"Because they know you're coming in," Tarin said.
Calist laughed and lifted the latch.
Feed had to be measured. Water troughs had to be filled. Bedding had to be turned and the worst of it carried out. A loose section of fence needed tying until someone could repair it properly.
Calist took two water buckets from the well.
Joric looked at him, then at the single bucket in his own hand.
Joric looked at the second full bucket.
He had always been difficult to tire compared with the others. Work in the smithy had made that more obvious as he grew. So had the simple fact that he almost never seemed to stay ill for long.
When half the village children caught the same winter fever, Calist had spent two miserable days in bed and a third arguing with Mara that he was well enough to get up.
She had made him stay there anyway.
Tarin had been sick for more than a week and still complained about the injustice of it whenever Calist mentioned the matter.
She was crouched near the fence, one hand resting against the wood.
Eryn pointed toward one of the goats.
Then the goat took three steps, and one hoof touched the ground more carefully than the others.
Eryn was already moving toward it.
"Probably caught it somewhere. Help me hold her."
The goat disagreed with this plan.
By the time Calist had both arms around it, Joric was laughing so hard that he had to put his bucket down.
"Come closer and I'll give her to you."
Eryn checked the hoof, found a small stone wedged near the edge, and worked it loose with patient fingers.
She stood and brushed dirt from her knees.
The goat walked away as though none of them had ever existed.
Her dark eyes were already fixed on a line of small tracks in the mud near the fence.
Eryn looked at him as if the answer were obvious.
Calist tried not to smile too much.
By midday, the animals were fed, the troughs were full, and most of the work was finished.
That was when Joric found the rake.
Joric lowered it like a spear.
Instead he picked up another wooden-handled tool and raised it in both hands.
"Your rake has teeth on the wrong end."
Tarin lasted perhaps ten seconds before taking up a broom and announcing that he would defeat both of them because neither understood tactics.
The battle moved exactly three paces before Calist backed into a pile of clean straw and disappeared into it.
Calist pushed himself upright with straw in his hair just as Garran Venn came around the side of the pen.
Then Calist sitting in the straw.
He was quiet for a moment.
Calist looked down at the straw.
"Good. When you've finished the war, the goats would still like to eat it."
"You will be if someone steps on that and breaks the handle. Tools are tools, even when you're bored."
His voice was firm, but there was no real anger in it.
Then he glanced toward Eryn and Nalia, both of whom were trying very hard not to laugh.
"And you two can help them put back whatever they scatter. Watching foolishness does not make you innocent of enjoying it."
"Exactly. You had every chance to stop them."
"No. But I was also an idiot at your age. That is not the defense you think it is."
The work took another half hour.
That evening, Calist found a piece of straw in his hair while eating supper.
Alden noticed him pull it free.
Calist set the straw beside his bowl.
Mara looked at him across the table.
"This is a village," Alden said. "There is no 'already.'"
"He said no tools were broken. I decided that was close enough to praise."
"And you heroically tried to stop him?"
Supper was a thick vegetable stew with a little smoked meat cut through it, dark bread, and the last of a soft cheese Mara had traded for with another household two days earlier.
No one had counted what the cheese was worth.
Mara had spent half a morning treating that household's youngest child when a cough had settled badly in his chest. The cheese had appeared on their table later.
That was simply how things happened.
After the bowls were empty, Alden remained at the table with a small iron fitting in his hand.
Calist recognized it as part of a shovel socket.
"Why didn't you finish that at the forge?"
"Because I wanted to see whether you'd notice this."
Then he saw a thin dark line near one edge.
"Repairing something isn't the same as pretending nothing happened to it. You need to know what the piece does, where the strain goes, and whether the repair will hold when someone actually uses it."
He tapped the crack with one fingernail.
"This? Fine. Clean it. Heat it properly. Close it. It'll work for years."
He turned the fitting and tapped another place.
"If the crack were here, I'd make a new one."
He liked these explanations more now than he had when he was small.
Perhaps because Alden had stopped giving him only the answers and started expecting him to understand the reasons.
Mara cleared part of the table and brought over three bundles of dried plants.
"Since you're both determined to keep working after supper."
"I have suddenly remembered something in the forge."
Mara placed the bundles in front of them.
"Separate those. Leaves here. Flowers here. Stems there. Anything blackened or damp goes out."
Calist picked up the first bundle.
Alden reached for the bread knife.
"Only if you let him make your medicine."
"Tarin knew after I showed him once," Mara said.
Mara took the stem from him and turned it between her fingers.
"Look at the leaves. Not the shape. The underside."
He put it in the correct pile.
Calist was not bad at the work.
He simply had to learn it through repetition in a way Tarin never seemed to.
Mara could show Tarin two nearly identical leaves and months later he would remember which one smelled sharper when crushed, which flowered first, and which became useless if gathered after rain.
Calist remembered the things he used often.
The rest had a habit of escaping him.
Outside, the village had grown quiet.
Someone closed a stable door. A dog barked once and stopped. Farther away, a hammer rang twice from a shed before whoever held it apparently decided the work could wait until morning.
He liked stories about roads he had never seen.
He liked hearing Corvin describe cities large enough to lose yourself in.
But there was something about the familiar quiet after supper that settled into him differently.
Almost every light in every window belonged to someone he knew.
Nothing beyond the village had ever felt like that.
Two mornings later, Mara sent Calist into the woods with Tarin and Eryn.
"The lower baskets are for mushrooms," she said. "The tall one is for herbs. Do not mix them."
Calist took one of the baskets.
Tarin already had the taller basket over one arm.
Eryn adjusted the strap of the small bow across her back.
"Can we go before you two become old men?"
The morning was cool beneath the trees. Sunlight came through in broken patches, catching on wet leaves and the pale tops of mushrooms pushing through the soil.
They stayed near the familiar gathering paths, far from the deeper parts of the old woods.
Mara had asked for two kinds of herb, a bitter root that grew near damp ground, and as many edible mushrooms as they could find without guessing.
Tarin found the first useful plants before Calist had finished deciding whether they were the right ones.
"Those aren't ready," Eryn said from several paces away.
"Then why are you looking at them?"
"Because I like knowing where they'll be later."
"You spent five minutes looking at bird tracks yesterday."
They worked slowly through the morning.
Calist knew the common mushrooms well enough. Brown caps beneath the old oak roots. Small pale clusters near dead wood. One broad red-brown kind Mara sliced and dried for winter stews.
Then he found another cluster beneath a fallen branch.
He crouched and cut three at the stems.
Tarin's voice came from behind him.
Tarin crouched beside him and took one.
There was something sharp beneath the earth smell.
"Not deadly," Tarin said. "Mara said you'd spend half the night being sick and the other half wishing your head would fall off."
Calist looked at the mushrooms in his hand.
Tarin looked at the open basket beside Calist's knee.
"You nearly poisoned the village. I think everyone gets an opinion."
"That is not the defense you think it is."
A little later, Eryn stopped so suddenly that Calist nearly walked into her.
Eryn looked toward a patch of brush ahead.
For several seconds, Calist saw nothing.
Then something brown moved between the leaves.
Only part of it was visible at first: one ear, the line of its neck, the dark shine of an eye.
The herbs might as well have ceased to exist.
She crouched without being told and watched the animal pick its way between the trees.
Where the deer placed its feet.
The faint movement of branches before its body passed beneath them.
Eryn touched two fingers to the ground after it disappeared.
That was all they told him.
"Smaller," Eryn said. "And lighter. See how deep they are?"
Calist nodded as though he did.
"Come on. We still need the bitter root."
Tarin waited until she was several paces away.
"You saw a hole in the mud."
That evening, Alden waited until Calist had nearly finished eating before he spoke.
"Garran and I are going to town in three days."
Calist's spoon stopped halfway to his mouth.
"We're low on good iron. Garran has hides and finished leather to take. Tessa has clothwork. A few others have things to send with us."
"Far enough that asking every question tonight won't make us arrive sooner."
For a moment, Calist forgot every question he had intended to ask.
"If you'd rather stay here and sort mushrooms with your mother—"
"Tarin told Joric. Joric told half the village."
Outside, beyond the familiar dark roofs and the quiet road, somewhere Calist had never been was waiting.
For once, he knew exactly when he would be allowed to go there.

blocks.text: Three days later, Calist was awake before Alden came to wake him.
The village wagon stood near the smithy in the grey light before sunrise.
It belonged to the village more than to any one household. Most of the year it carried sacks at harvest, timber, barrels, tools, or anything else too heavy or awkward to move by hand.
The ox harnessed to it spent far more time helping in the fields than traveling the road.
They had little reason to keep horses of their own. Horses were useful to people who needed to move quickly and often. The village usually needed neither.
Today, no one was in a hurry.
Dew still silvered the grass beside the road, and the cool air smelled of damp earth and wood smoke.
Garran tightened the last strap across a stack of bundled hides while Alden checked one of the wheels.
Joric arrived with a small pack and the expression of someone who had dressed before fully waking. Nalia came after him, then Eryn with Tessa at her side.
Tessa handed Garran a wrapped bundle.
"These go to Mira Pell. Not Heddan Rell."
Calist climbed into the back of the wagon beside Joric.
"I know. How long until we get there?"
"About a third of the day, with the rests. Longer if the ox decides otherwise."
Joric leaned against a bundle of leather.
"Can we ask if we're there yet?"
The wagon started with a wooden groan.
Mara stood outside their house with one hand raised until a bend in the road hid her from view.
Calist kept looking back for another few moments anyway.
For the first time in his life, he was following it somewhere.
He had expected that to feel faster.
The ox walked at the same patient pace whether Calist was excited or not.
The wheels creaked. Harness leather shifted. Birds called from the hedges.
They passed fields Calist had seen from a distance before, then fields he had not.
"Corvin once told us about a wagon that broke an axle near a river bend," Calist said.
"Because that bend looks like the one he described."
"Did he describe what it looked like?"
Eryn smiled from the other side of the wagon.
A little later they passed a ditch, which reminded Calist of the soldier who had fallen into one while chasing goblins years earlier.
A low hill reminded him of something Corvin had once said about autumn grass farther north.
A stand of old willows somehow reminded him of the ferry story, though even Calist admitted there was no ferry anywhere nearby.
By the fourth story, Nalia asked, "Does everything on this road remind you of something someone told you?"
Joric pointed at an ordinary tree.
They stopped several times along the way.
The stops were not for the children.

The ox needed water, grass, and a chance to stand without the wagon pulling behind it. Garran loosened part of the harness. Alden checked the wheels. The children stretched their legs, ate bread and hard cheese, and were repeatedly told not to wander too far from the road.
The most dramatic event of the journey was Joric nearly sitting in a patch of thistles.
Calist thought the entire trip was wonderful.
Later in the morning, the first roofs appeared ahead.

A pair of weathered stone posts and open wooden gates marked the town's edge. Beyond them, the road widened and another road joined it. Carts came from both directions, and people Calist did not know walked past without greeting him.

The quiet rhythm of the wagon disappeared beneath wheels on hard-packed road, voices, hammering, animals, and the occasional shout from a stall. The smells changed too: dust and fields gave way to horse, wood smoke, hot metal, leather, and somewhere ahead, baking bread.
Alden had told him several times that the town was small.

There were more buildings along one street than Calist could see from the center of his entire village. Some had upper floors. Signs hung above doors. Stalls stood beneath cloth awnings. Smoke rose from workshops he could not identify by smell alone.
A bell rang somewhere beyond the roofs.
Calist almost missed Garran telling him to climb down.
"If you stare with your mouth open, someone will charge you for it," Garran said.
Their first stop was an iron yard off the market square.
Instead there were racks of bars, bundles of rod, rough plates, broken pieces meant for remelting, crates of nails, and metal in shapes Alden never kept in such quantities.
Heddan Rell greeted Alden by name and Garran with a complaint about the smell of hides.
Garran told him the hides smelled better than he did.
The children helped unload what they had brought while the adults talked weights, quality, and prices.
Calist tried to listen to everything at once.
Alden picked up one iron bar, checked its edge, then struck it lightly against another.
"You picked a good week. It may cost more again by next month."
Heddan lowered his voice only a little.
Garran stopped checking a bundle of straps.
"That's what the traders say. More crossings. More farms hit. A few small posts too. Nothing like a war. Not yet."

"One says their winter was bad enough that whole districts lost stores. Another says they're short of grazing land and good fields. Another says some lord over there decided our side looks richer than his."
Alden looked down at the iron again.
"Rumors get cheaper the farther they travel."
That ended the serious part of the conversation.
They went back to arguing over price.
A far border. More attacks. A neighboring kingdom he had never seen.
Even trouble could exist beyond the horizon.
By the time the first deals were settled, Garran finally turned toward the four children.
Alden held up one finger before any of them could move.
"Together," Alden repeated. "Not two here and two somewhere else. Not 'we could still see them from the corner.' Together."
"If you get lost, come here. Heddan knows us."
Heddan raised a hand without looking up from his ledger.
"Or ask for Mira Pell. She keeps the bread shop on the west side of the square. She knows us too."
"Meeting point is the wagon," Alden said. "Two hours. If you're late, you spend the ride home walking beside it."
Garran handed each of them a few copper coins.
Calist stared at the money in his palm.
"Whatever small useless thing convinces you the trip was worth making," Garran said. "Or food. Preferably food."
Eryn closed her fingers around hers.
Then the four of them were on their own.
In the village, an adult was never more than a few houses away, and almost every adult knew exactly who they were.
Here, most people did not care.
They crossed the square twice before agreeing on a direction.
Joric bought a twisted piece of honeyed bread before they had been free for ten minutes.
Nalia spent one copper on a narrow blue ribbon and then spent the next five minutes insisting she had not wasted it.
Eryn stopped at every stall with knives, hunting gear, feathers, horn, or leatherwork.

There were colored glass beads. Small carved animals. Spices that made him sneeze. Books he could not afford even if all four of them combined their money. Tiny painted figures of soldiers, none of whom looked as tired as the real soldiers Calist knew.
He stopped so suddenly that Joric walked into his back.
Calist pointed before remembering that pointing at people was rude.
The dwarf stood behind a metalwork stall near the edge of the square.

He was much shorter than Alden, but broad enough through the shoulders that the difference in height did not make him look small. His beard was tied into two thick braids to keep it away from his work, and his hands looked almost too large for the delicate ring he was adjusting with a tiny pair of pliers.
The dwarf's eyes narrowed with amusement.
"Bram Ordek. There. Now you've met one too. Come look at the work. It's more interesting."
Calist did not need to be invited twice.
The stall was full of metal things that had almost no practical reason to exist.
Rings. Pendants. Small chains. Decorative clasps. Tiny animals made from twisted wire. Buckles engraved with patterns too fine for Calist to imagine doing with Alden's ordinary tools.
He picked up a small copper pendant and turned it over.
The back was almost as clean as the front.
That earned Calist a different look.
Bram took the pendant and showed him the edge.
"Because the seam is where you aren't looking. Heat, clean surfaces, and patience. Mostly patience."
"My father says bad joins show when the piece is under strain."
Beside him, Eryn had gone quiet.
The pendant was small and silver-colored, shaped like a narrow leaf with a tiny copper arrow worked across it. Nothing about it was extravagant. The detail was simply very fine.
Eryn ran one thumb over the edge.
Eryn's expression changed only a little.
It was enough for Calist to notice.
The few coins Garran had given them would not come close.
Eryn set the necklace back carefully.
Bram nodded as though this happened often.
"Metal keeps better than bread. It'll exist somewhere."
Eryn moved on to a set of small hunting clasps.
Calist looked at the necklace once more before following her.
He did remember exactly which one it had been.
They still had nearly half their time left when the trouble began.
It started with laughter behind them.
Four town boys stood near a stack of empty crates. They were around the same age, perhaps one or two years older at most.
One looked at the dust dried along Joric's trouser leg.
Another boy wrinkled his nose dramatically.
Their clothes were cleaner than the village children's, but not fine. They were ordinary town boys, not little nobles. They simply had not spent a third of the day behind an ox on a dusty road.
Nalia looked at the boy who had spoken.
Eryn made a choking sound that might have been a laugh.
Calist already knew where this was going.
"You should try working sometime. Might improve the smell."
The first boy shoved Joric in the chest.
Then everyone made bad decisions at once.
One of the town boys swung at Joric.
Calist stepped between them and took the blow high on his shoulder.
He also knew what it felt like to drop a heavy bar against himself, to take a kick from an annoyed goat, to slip carrying wood, or to finish a day's work with bruises he had forgotten receiving.
It was not enough to make him move.
Calist remembered Corvin nudging his foot into place years earlier.
The second shove did even less.
Calist pushed him backward into the crates.
Someone grabbed Calist from the side.
Joric threw himself at that someone with more enthusiasm than skill.
Nalia shouted something Calist did not hear and hit another boy with her folded market bag.
She did not try to overpower anyone.
A boy lunged toward her. Eryn slipped aside and stuck out a foot. He stumbled.
Before he recovered, a small stone struck him sharply in the shin.
Eryn already had another in her hand.
Calist had watched her hit knotholes with pebbles from farther away than this.
He knew what came next before the boy did.
The stone struck between his legs.
He folded with a sound that made every boy in the street instinctively wince.
Another town boy came at Calist.
That was the strange advantage he had.
He was not faster than Eryn. He was not especially clever about fighting. But he knew he could take a hit and still be there afterward.
A punch caught his ribs. Another glanced from his forearm. He closed the distance, got both hands on the boy's coat, and shoved hard.
The boy stumbled into his friend just as Eryn moved around Calist's other side.
Neither of them had planned it.
When someone tried to get around Calist, Eryn was there first. When one of them turned toward her, Calist got in the way. She moved quickly where he held ground.
Joric and Nalia did their best in the confusion, both too stubborn to leave and too inexperienced to do anything gracefully.
The town boys were not weak.
They were simply surprised by how difficult the village children were to put down.

Calist and the others spent their days carrying water, splitting wood, moving sacks, wrestling stubborn animals, walking fields, and working until a job was finished because there was no one else to finish it for them.
That did not make them trained fighters.
It did make them hard to bully.
For several confused moments the street became a knot of elbows, dust, shouting, and bad decisions.
Calist took another hit that split the inside of his lip against his teeth.
He caught the boy by the front of his coat.
The voice stopped him more effectively than a punch.
Corvin Hale stood in the street with two soldiers beside him.

Calist knew both of them from the smithy. Merek Dain had once spent an entire afternoon complaining while Alden repaired three broken buckles on the same harness. Oren Voss was the soldier who always brought apples for the village children and then pretended he had not.
For a moment no one moved.
Corvin looked at Calist's bleeding lip.
Then at Joric half-kneeling on another boy's coat.
Then at Nalia gripping her market bag like a club.
Then at Eryn, who still had a stone in one hand.
Finally he looked at the boy bent over several paces away.
"I am going to regret asking," Corvin said. "What happened?"
One of the town boys pointed at her.
Merek turned his head and coughed into one fist.
Calist strongly suspected he was hiding a laugh.
The town boys were suddenly very interested in leaving.
Corvin let them go after making certain none of them was badly hurt.
Then he looked at the four children he knew.
There were bruises. Scraped hands. Calist's lip.
"Back to the people you came here with."
"You may explain that to them. I'm sure they'll be fascinated by the distinction."
Alden was not fascinated by the distinction.
They listened while the four children explained what had happened, sometimes all at once, until Alden finally held up one hand.
Corvin stood beside the wagon with Merek and Oren, looking much too comfortable for someone responsible for returning them.
Garran closed his eyes for a moment.
Oren looked very carefully at the sky.
"I taught her to aim," Garran said at last. "I may regret that."
"That was not permission to feel proud."
"For what it's worth, they weren't losing."
Only then did Calist realize why Corvin was in town at all.
Several military packs and supply crates stood near the soldiers' horses. A leather case of papers was strapped behind Corvin's saddle.
"Long enough to collect supplies and deliver reports," Corvin said. "Then we're back on the road."
Calist immediately wanted to ask what reports.
Alden saw it happen on his face.
"You four wanted something to do. Now you have it."
"Water first. The ox needs it before we leave. Full bucket, not half because you're tired."
Garran pointed toward the goods stacked beside the wagon.
"Then those crates get loaded. Metal low and toward the center. Food above it. Leather where it stays dry."
Nalia stared at one of the iron-filled crates.
Calist wiped the blood from his lip with the back of his hand.
"And since you're the one who likes proving how much you can carry, you can start with that one."
"I remember saying something once about conquering the border after you finished the floor."
Calist bent, got both hands under the crate, and lifted.
It was heavier than he expected.
Eryn immediately took the other side without being asked.
For one second they looked at each other.
Then they carried it toward the wagon together.
Behind them, Joric and Nalia started toward the well with the buckets.
Which, Calist reflected, made it remarkably similar to being at home.
It also gave them plenty of time to discuss the battle.
At least, quietly enough that the adults standing on the other side of the wagon could pretend not to hear.
"You should have seen his face," Joric whispered as he returned with one of the water buckets. "When Calist pushed him into the crates."
"I did see it," Nalia said. "I was there."
Calist and Eryn lowered another crate into the wagon.
Eryn straightened and rubbed her hands together.
"Calist mostly stood there and got hit."
"You were very good at standing there."
Joric nearly dropped the bucket laughing.
Calist looked toward the animal tied nearby.
The ox chewed slowly and showed no interest in defending him.
"Because you kept running around everyone and attacking whatever they weren't protecting."
All three boys winced in perfect agreement.
Nalia carefully checked the small blue ribbon tucked into her market bag.
"We nearly got beaten through a street and you're worried about the ribbon?"
She folded the ribbon more carefully and tucked it deeper into the bag.
Joric sighed and looked toward the market.
"You told them they smelled worse than goats."
Calist lifted one end of another crate.
They all knew there had been other choices.
They also knew, with the uncomfortable certainty of people who had known one another most of their lives, that none of them would actually have made those choices once the shoving started.
Joric took the other end of the crate.
On the far side of the wagon, the adults were having a conversation of their own.
Corvin had unfolded a short list and was comparing it with the supplies beside Merek's horse.
"Salt, lamp oil, two bundles of cord, dried meat," he said. "We still need the grain sacks."
"Other side of the square," Oren said.
"You said that about the lamp oil."
Alden glanced toward the clouds gathering over the western roofs.
"I'm learning from your ox. Never hurry when the sky is making threats."
The children worked until the water was carried, the iron was packed low in the wagon, and the remaining provisions were wedged where they would not shift on the road.
Joric leaned against the wheel when they were done.
Joric closed his eyes in relief.
Then Garran said, "After that, we'll walk the market."
Alden gave them a long look.
"You're still being punished. That doesn't mean the entire trip has to be ruined."
"Very much together," Garran said. "With us this time."
Joric decided supervision was a small price to pay.
The market felt different with Alden and Garran walking behind them.
Just less like the four of them had somehow been released into another world without anyone watching.
Joric bought another piece of honeyed bread and was told this was becoming a poor use of money.
He answered that bread could not be a poor use of money because it was food.
Nalia found a small wooden comb and spent several minutes deciding whether it was worth another copper before keeping her coin instead.
Eryn stopped at a bowyer's stall long enough that Garran eventually had to remind her they were not buying a new bow.

Hinges with decorative leaves worked into the plates. Small knives with patterned handles. Buckles finer than anything needed for a work belt. Brass cups. Copper pins. Tiny tools whose purpose he could only guess.
They passed Bram Ordek's stall again.
The dwarf was speaking with a customer and did not notice them.
The leaf-and-arrow necklace was still hanging where Eryn had left it.
He looked at the narrow seam around the pendant.
Then at Bram's hands moving as he spoke.
Alden's voice came from several paces ahead.
Their last stop was Mira Pell's bakery on the west side of the square.
Calist smelled it before they reached the door.
Warm bread, browned crust, dried fruit, and something sweet he could not name filled the little shop.
Mira herself was a broad woman with flour on one sleeve and the habit of speaking while continuing three other tasks.
"Garran. You remembered Tessa's bundle this time."
Garran placed it on the counter.
Mira laughed and passed him a wrapped parcel in return.
"And this is for Nessa. Fresh this morning. Apples, dried berries, enough honey that she can't complain it's too plain."
"Of course she will. She's earned the right."

Calist knew Nessa Venn as Eryn's grandmother and as the oldest person in the village. She still insisted on doing more for herself than Mara thought sensible, but journeys like this had stopped being an option for her some time ago.
Mira added a second, smaller loaf.
By the time they stepped outside again, the light had changed.
The western clouds had thickened into one dark mass. Wind moved between the buildings in short cold gusts, lifting dust and tugging at awnings.
Alden looked at the sky for only a few seconds.
"Because we'd reach the worst stretch near dark, and I don't like those clouds."
The ox was nowhere in sight.

They took the wagon to a stable yard behind an inn near the southern gate. The stableman found space for the ox, helped them pull the wagon beneath a long lean-to, and promised the animal hay, water, and more respect than Garran usually showed it.
Garran said the ox was already becoming spoiled.
The children were delighted by the change of plan.
Spending one day away from home had already been extraordinary.
Spending the night made it something else entirely.
The inn was louder than any supper Calist had ever eaten at home.
People spoke over one another. Cups struck tables. A chair scraped every few moments. Someone near the hearth laughed loudly enough to make half the room look over.
Calist tried to watch everything until Alden told him to eat before the stew went cold.
Corvin, Merek, and Oren joined them not long afterward.
Apparently the weather had changed their plans too.
Oren dropped onto the bench beside Joric.
"I hear you've been fighting wars without us."
"The entire market probably knows by now," Merek said.
Eryn pointed her spoon at him.
The conversation stayed easy while the children were at the table.

Corvin told Alden which roads were in poor shape. Garran asked about leather prices near the fort. Oren complained about a cook who believed salt was a personal insult. Merek claimed Oren would eat boot leather if enough onion was put on it.
He also noticed that Alden asked nothing about the reports Corvin had mentioned earlier.
When the bowls were empty and the younger four had begun fighting sleep despite insisting they were not tired, Alden stood.
Garran handed Eryn the stable-yard lantern.
The wagon had been emptied enough to make room among the remaining bundles. Blankets went down over boards and folded sacks. It was not a bed.
To Calist, that made it better.
For several minutes the four of them whispered in the dark, replaying the day in fragments.
The boy Eryn had hit with the stone.
Eryn told Calist to stop moving because the wagon creaked every time he shifted.
He whispered that he was trying to get comfortable.
A few minutes later, her breathing became slow and even too.
He was too tired not to sleep.
He was also far too excited to manage it.
The day kept repeating behind his eyes.
Every time Calist thought he was finally drifting off, some other piece returned.
Much later, footsteps crossed the stable yard.
Alden and Garran had returned with Corvin, Merek, and Oren. Someone set down a lantern outside the wagon. Hay shifted as blankets were spread nearby.
Calist stared into the darkness above him.
"Bad enough that the reports are real. Not bad enough that I'd call it war."
Merek's voice came next, lower than Calist was used to hearing it.
"Three crossings we know of this month. Two farms stripped. One burned after the family fled. A patrol traded arrows with men on the other side two days ago."
"Nobody got close enough to ask," Oren said. "But they weren't hungry peasants wandering over a line by mistake."
Calist could picture his father's face without seeing it.
"One raid. Then another. Patrols answer. Someone sends more men because the first lot wasn't enough. Then someone dies who matters to the wrong person."
For a while only the ox could be heard shifting in its stall.
Then Corvin said, "The command knows. That's what some of my reports are about. For now we're watching it. That's all I can tell you because that's all I know."
The conversation moved on after that, quieter still.
Calist did not hear every word.
He did not try to move closer.
He knew what would happen if he sat up and asked questions.
Alden would tell him to sleep.
Corvin would tell him nothing he had not already heard.
The excitement of the day had not vanished.
It had simply gained something heavier beside it.
Morning made the previous night's worry feel strangely distant.
The clouds had passed without much more than a short rain. The road shone wet beneath a pale sky, and the ox looked deeply unimpressed by being harnessed again.
Calist climbed into the wagon expecting the same slow journey home.
Then Corvin led three saddled horses into the yard.
"Part of the way," Corvin said. "Our road runs past your village before we turn for the fort."
"We considered tying your wagon behind us."
"Try it and I'll charge you for the axle."
The journey remained exactly as uneventful as the day before.
No ambush waited beyond the gate. No wheel broke. No neighboring army appeared over a hill.
There was only wet road, fields, hedges, and the patient rhythm of the ox.
With the soldiers beside them, however, the time passed differently.
Calist asked questions until Corvin threatened to ride ahead.
Joric asked whether cavalry training included learning how not to fall off while sleeping.
Merek said that was Oren's greatest military skill.
Oren denied having ever fallen asleep on a horse.
His horse chose that moment to stumble slightly over a rut.
At one of the rests, Eryn showed Corvin how far she could hit a tree with a pebble.
Corvin watched the stone strike exactly where she had pointed.
"You really did teach her to aim."
The familiar hills returned one by one.
Then the old woods in the distance.
By early afternoon, the first roofs of the village appeared.
Calist had been gone barely more than a day.
The sight still settled something in him.
Corvin and the soldiers stopped only long enough for Oren to hand three apples to children who had come running toward the road, while insisting the fruit had somehow fallen from his saddlebag.
Then Corvin raised one hand to Alden.
"We'll see you on the next pass."
"Try to keep the same horse alive until then."
Calist watched the three riders continue along the road until they reached the turn that would eventually take them toward the fort.
Then Alden tapped the side of the wagon.
"Don't stare too long. We still have to unload it."
Unloading did not remain their job for long.
A loaded village wagon returning from town attracted people almost immediately.

Someone came for the sack of salt. Someone else helped Alden with the iron. Tessa appeared before Garran had finished loosening the first leather bundle. Tarin arrived with two other children and demanded a complete account of everything that had happened before lifting anything at all.
The story continued while they worked.

Crates were carried toward the smithy. Cloth and thread went to Tessa. A small sack of seed changed hands twice before reaching the right household. Oil, nails, salt, dried fruit, and other purchases disappeared through the village almost as quickly as they came off the wagon.
No one stood beside the load counting who had paid for what.
People simply knew what had been needed and where it belonged.
The children were sent off with the smaller things.
Nalia carried sewing needles and a packet of buttons to Tessa.
Joric and Tarin took salt and lamp oil toward two houses farther down the road.
Calist and Eryn were given Mira Pell's wrapped fruit bread.
"Straight to your grandmother," Garran told Eryn.
They carried it together to Nessa Venn's house near the far end of the village.
Nessa was sitting outside beneath a blanket despite the mild afternoon, sorting beans into a shallow bowl.
She looked up as they approached.
"That woman puts too much honey in everything."
Eryn kissed her grandmother's cheek and set the bread beside her.
Nessa looked past her at Calist.
"Good. Then I don't need to scold you."
She broke one bean between her fingers and dropped it into the discard bowl.
Calist decided immediately that Nessa was his favorite elder.
They stayed only long enough to tell a shortened version before Eryn remembered they still had work waiting.
By then the sun had begun to lower.
The village slowly settled around them.
Doors closed against the cooler evening air. Animals were brought in. Smoke rose from chimneys. The noise around the wagon faded as the last goods found their places.
One by one, people went home.
Mara had barely put supper on the table before Calist started talking.
He told her about the road first.
Alden sat down across from him.

"His work was tiny. Not bad tiny. Fine. He had chains where you could barely see how the links were closed, and pendants with joins hidden inside the edges, and this little copper animal made from wire that—"
Mara smiled and let him continue.
He told her about the inn.
He nearly managed to skip the fight.
Then Mara looked at his lip.
Alden ate another spoonful of stew.
He was no help at all.
Mara slowly put down her spoon.
By the time Calist finished explaining, Alden had to cover his mouth when Mara reached the part involving Eryn's second stone.
"You are not laughing," Mara told him.
Calist decided the safest thing was to eat.
Later, once the story had been told properly and Mara had inspected his lip despite his insistence that it was already fine, the house became quiet again.
The kind Calist had missed without knowing he would.
He went to bed tired enough that sleep should have come immediately.
Mostly, he thought about Bram's stall.
The way something made of metal could be useful for nothing at all and still be worth making because someone had made it beautifully.
Then he remembered Eryn holding the necklace.
The way she had asked the price and put it back without complaint.
He did not have enough money to buy something like that.
That thought bothered him for perhaps a minute.
Or at least, he was trying to become one.
Maybe buying it was not the point.
Someday, he decided, he would learn to make one himself.
Something Eryn would look at the same way.
For once, the future he imagined did not contain a sword, a distant road, or a soldier's story.
It contained a small piece of metal in his hands.
And enough skill to make it beautiful.
