blocks.text: The thought did not become a necklace the next morning.
It did not become anything for quite a while.
The days stayed long and warm. Brief rains darkened the packed earth around the smithy and left the gardens shining; on dry afternoons dust clung to boots and wagon wheels.

The forge still needed water. Animals still needed feeding. Fields still needed hands. Hinges broke, knives dulled, wheels loosened, and every time Calist thought he had found an afternoon with nothing pressing to do, someone found something for him.
The leaf-and-arrow pendant stayed in his memory anyway.
Not merely because the dwarf had made something beautiful.
Calist had watched Alden make hundreds of things that worked exactly as they should. He understood that kind of skill better every year.
Bram had shown him something else.
Precision so fine that Calist had not even known to look for it until he saw it.
It was simply difficult to look at the work he already knew and remain satisfied with knowing only that much.

One evening, several weeks after the town trip, the day's fire had burned down to a red bed beneath the forge. Cooler air came through the open doors carrying the smell of cut grass, but inside there was still charcoal, hot iron, and the damp mineral smell of the quench bucket. Hammers and tongs hung dark against the wall, each in a place Calist knew well enough to find without looking.
Alden was cleaning the face of a hammer when Calist stopped beside the workbench.
Alden kept rubbing the metal with an oiled cloth.
Calist immediately realized how the word sounded.
Calist leaned one hand against the bench.
"I don't want to only fetch things and hold things anymore."
"I want to make things people will actually use. Without you doing the important part afterward."
His father studied him for long enough that Calist became aware of how hot the forge still was despite the evening air.
He had not prepared an answer.
He said none of those things.
There were other reasons now anyway.
He had watched adults stop asking him merely to carry things and start trusting him to finish small jobs. He had liked the difference more than he expected.
He liked being the person someone looked for when something heavy had to move.
He wanted there to be more things people could look for him to do.
"I want to be useful," he said.
That answer seemed to satisfy him more.
Alden picked up the hammer again.
"Then you make them again until they aren't bad."
"If you rush because you want to get to the interesting work, you'll spend twice as long doing the boring work again."
Calist looked at the hammer in his father's hand.
Alden handed him the oily cloth.
Apparently proper teaching began with cleaning someone else's hammer.
Alden had not been joking about the hinges.
The first pair did not match.
The second matched only if Calist held them far enough apart.
Alden made him produce another pair anyway.
Small repairs in places where a mistake would be annoying rather than dangerous.
He did not always fix what was wrong.
Sometimes he simply handed the piece back.
Calist learned to hate that word.
He also learned that it usually meant Alden believed he could do better without being shown how.
By late summer, the first thing Calist made entirely himself that someone genuinely needed was a gate hook.
It was not even especially interesting.
It was a thick piece of iron bent to hold a gate closed against animals that had no respect for gates.
Calist still stared at it as though it were a sword fit for a king.
Alden turned it over in his hand.
His father inspected the curve, then the flattened end where the nail holes had been punched.
One hole sat slightly farther from the edge than the other.
Alden ran his thumb over it.
"The bend is thick enough. The holes aren't close enough to the edge to split it. And it doesn't need to look even."
Calist looked down at the hook again.
"Then stop trying to give me more work."
That afternoon Calist carried it to one of the pens near the far side of the village.
The old hook there had worn thin where it rubbed against the staple. Joric was already nearby, helping one of the farmers replace a cracked section of fence.
Calist removed the old fitting, set the new one, and drove the nails home.
When he was finished, he closed the gate.
The hook dropped neatly into place.
"Are you planning to spend the rest of the day doing that?"
Nalia came around the pen carrying a short stack of cut boards.
Calist tried not to sound too pleased.
Nalia touched the iron with one finger.
Nalia's green eyes stayed on the hook.
It would spend the next several years being rained on, struck by a gate, rubbed by dirty hands, and entirely ignored unless it broke.
For some reason, she kept looking at it.
Then she said, quietly enough that Calist almost missed it,
"I want to be able to say that."
Joric looked from Nalia to the hook.
"I don't want to make a hook."
"Then what do you want to make?"
She picked up the boards again.
Once Calist began paying attention to his own work differently, he started noticing the same change in his friends.
Tarin was easiest to notice because he was almost always at Calist's house.
He had stopped arriving as a visitor often enough that Mara sometimes opened the door, handed him a basket, and told him what needed gathering before he had properly said hello.
One afternoon Calist came in from the forge and found Tarin at the table grinding dried leaves with a stone pestle while Mara measured beeswax beside him.
A much younger girl from another household sat on a stool between them, carefully pulling damaged leaves from a pile.
He held up the leaf she had almost discarded.
"The brown edge is fine. Feel it. Dry, not soft."
Tarin put it back into the good pile.
"If it's damp or black underneath, then it goes."
The girl nodded with enormous seriousness.
"Put the water down before you drop it."
The little girl was not Tarin's sister.
No one in the room behaved as though that mattered.
A few days later Alden sent Calist across the fields with a repaired hoe.
He found Joric before he found the owner.
Joric was knee-deep in a ditch beside the field, clearing mud and weeds from the narrow channel that carried rainwater away from the crops. Two younger boys were working farther along under his eye.
One of them had stopped working entirely to watch a beetle crawl over his hand.
"If the beetle clears more ditch than you do, I'm giving it your supper," Joric called.
The boy immediately returned to work.
Joric climbed out of the ditch.
He took the hoe, checked the repaired socket, and swung it once experimentally.
Joric handed the tool to one of the younger boys.
"Take that to Halven. Don't swing it at anything with legs."
Joric looked toward the other boy, who had discovered something else fascinating in the mud.
Joric went back into the ditch.
There was no single job that seemed to belong to him.
Animals one day. Fields the next. Fences, feed, harvest, wagons, drainage, whatever needed hands.
Joric seemed perfectly content with that.
Calist crossed Eryn's path just as often without either of them arranging it.
Alden sharpened and repaired enough of the hunters' tools that there was always something to take or collect.
One afternoon Calist carried a freshly sharpened skinning knife to Garran's yard and found a deer hanging beneath the shade behind the house.
Harlan and Bren were working nearby.
Her sleeves were rolled above her elbows. There was blood on both hands and a dark streak across one forearm.
Calist stopped for half a second.
She wiped one hand before taking it from him.
Eryn tested the edge lightly against her thumb, then handed it to him hilt first.
Calist felt a small spark of pride before remembering that Alden had sharpened this one.
Her movements were slower than Harlan's but sure enough that he did not need to correct every cut.
"Are you going to stand there all afternoon?" she asked.
"That's what I'm trying for," Calist said.
He immediately wished he had not said it out loud.
She only smiled and went back to work.
Nalia began appearing at the smithy for different reasons too.
Alden looked up from the anvil.
Alden stared at the distance between them.
Eventually she found the cracked metal pin on the workbench herself.
"Tell Tessa I'll bring it when I've fitted the new end."
Nalia looked at the part rather than leaving.
Alden turned it so she could see the worn edge.
"Because the wooden arm has started sitting crooked. If I only replace this, you'll be back with another broken one."
"I can look at it. Someone who works wood every day would be better."
A few weeks later she came back carrying a narrow chisel whose edge had been chipped.
This time no one had sent her to ask what it was.
Calist looked over from the bench.
"You did the same thing Eryn does."
"The thing where you say nothing after obviously thinking something."
"I can regrind it. You chip it again this quickly and I'll make you do it yourself."
Then he moved aside at the bench.
Calist returned to his own work.
Behind him, Alden began explaining angles to someone else's child exactly as he had once explained them to Calist.
By the time the main harvest began, Calist no longer needed to think about how much the village's work crossed from one household to another.
Harvest made the truth impossible to miss anyway.
For days, almost everything that could wait did wait.

The forge stayed open because tools still broke, but Alden spent as much time in the fields as he did at the anvil. Mara gathered and dried what needed gathering, then joined the others when she could. Tessa worked until there was enough light to sew and then spent the remaining hours wherever another pair of hands was useful. Garran moved between animals, leather, wagons, and fields.
The children and older youths moved with them.
The youngest carried water, gathered dropped stalks, watched smaller children, or did whatever could be done without getting beneath the feet of carts and animals.
Calist's group had become old enough to be trusted with more.
That did not stop adults from telling them what they were doing wrong.
It only meant the corrections came while they were already doing real work.
When the last of the main harvest was finally safe, the village held its harvest feast.
The day was dry and bright, with a light wind moving chaff through the stubbled fields. The air still smelled faintly of cut grain, but the evenings had begun to cool.
No one household could have hosted it.

Some were carried whole from houses. Others were nothing more than boards laid over trestles. Benches followed. Chairs. Stools. Lanterns. Heavy cooking pots. Baskets of bread. Jugs. Blankets for the evening. Someone dragged out a long awning in case the weather changed. Someone else produced two strings of old colored cloth that had apparently decorated every harvest feast since before Calist was born.
By midday, the open space near the center of the village looked as though half the houses had emptied themselves into it.
Calist carried one end of a table with Joric.
"Move," Calist said as one darted in front of his feet.
The child moved exactly far enough to be in Joric's way instead.
Calist and Joric finally put the table down.
Across the clearing, Garran was preventing another group of children from climbing a cart that had been brought over to carry barrels.
Joric watched him for a moment.
Nessa Venn had been given the most comfortable chair anyone could find.
She had also been placed beneath shade, wrapped in a blanket she insisted she did not need, and provided with a small table beside her before she had managed to object to any of it.
As the oldest person in the village, Nessa received this treatment every year.
As the best cook in the village, she immediately used the position to command everyone within hearing distance.
"More water in that pot. Not that much. Do you intend to feed soup to the ground?"
"Here," Tarin called from behind two other children.
"Good. Mara has trained one of you properly."
Calist was carrying firewood past them.
"You nearly fed us the wrong mushrooms."
"And I am old. My memory is one of the few things people still let me carry."
Calist put down the wood and stayed.
There were always children around Nessa these days.

She could no longer follow them through the fields or walk to town, but she could sit with a knife and show small hands how thin roots needed to be cut. She could smell a pot and know what was missing. She knew which fruits kept longest, how much salt a crock needed, what could replace an ingredient when stores ran low, and which mistakes could be eaten anyway if no one admitted making them.
The children did the reaching, carrying, cutting, stirring, fetching, and running.
Nessa supplied the knowledge and enough criticism to keep all of them awake.
A little girl beside her was peeling a root far too thickly.
"We want food in the pot, not on the peel."
Calist sat on an overturned bucket and began splitting the smaller pieces of firewood.
One of the children asked why everyone in the village had to help with everything.
"Because wheat has never cared what a man's usual work is."
The boy seemed to consider this.
Nessa looked toward Alden, who was helping move another table at the far end of the clearing.
"It was always like that here, more or less. We were never rich enough in people to pretend otherwise."
"The war taught us to be better at it."
"There. Now I've caught one of them."
Nessa looked at the younger children around her.
"Compared with me, all of you are making a poor argument."
Nessa settled more comfortably into the chair.
"When the crown called the young men, your father went with them. So did several others."
He had never heard Nessa tell it.

"They didn't take the work with them," she continued. "Fields still needed planting. Animals still needed tending. Roofs still leaked. Tools still broke. Winter still arrived because apparently nobody had informed winter that we were short of hands."
A few of the older children smiled.

"Harder than most of you have seen. The older men did work they had already begun giving to younger backs. Women who already had more than enough to do took on still more. Older children worked beside us instead of only under us. We planted less in some places because there were not enough hands to manage everything. Repairs waited. Everyone was tired."
He had never thought much about what the village had been doing while his father was away fighting.
She pointed toward the cooking pot.
"One person knowing how to do something is useful. Only one person knowing it is dangerous."
"Mara should know more about herbs than you. For now."
"If you keep following her around, she'll have to work hard to stay ahead of you."

"But if Mara falls ill tomorrow," Nessa continued, "the village should not suddenly forget what helps a fever. Alden should be the best smith here. That doesn't mean every simple repair must wait if he breaks an arm. Harlan should track better than the rest of us. That doesn't mean nobody else should know which way a deer went."
"We helped each other before the war. After it, we became less willing to let one pair of hands be the only pair that knew how to keep something going."
Calist looked at the children around her.
Tarin was correcting a bundle of herbs.
Calist himself had spent the morning carrying tables and the afternoon cutting wood despite being a smith's son.
None of it had ever seemed like a lesson.
Perhaps that was why all of them had learned so much of it.
Nessa pointed the root at him.
"And if you're finished listening, that pot still needs your firewood."
By evening the elders had been seated together near the warmest fire.
No rule said they had to sit there.

The best-backed chairs appeared beneath them. Plates reached them before they had to stand. Cups were refilled before they were empty. When one of the older men tried to carry his own stool, two younger adults took it from him while he complained that his arms had not fallen off yet.
Nessa complained more than any of them.

She had spent most of a lifetime feeding people, remembering what had worked in difficult years, settling arguments, caring for children who were now old enough to have children of their own, and helping keep the village alive when too many younger hands had been elsewhere.
Nobody was going to let her carry a bench merely because she remained convinced she could.

There was more food than Calist had seen gathered in one place all year, though much of it was simple. Bread. Root vegetables. Stew. Roasted meat. Cheese. Preserved fruit opened because this was exactly the sort of day it had been preserved for.
Joric ate enough that Nessa eventually told him she had not survived a war just to watch him empty the village stores alone.
He considered that a challenge until three adults told him it was not.
There was dancing, some of it better than the rest.
Children ran between the tables until someone older caught them and redirected them toward games farther from the fires.
The second time, the little boy he stopped stared up at him and said,
"Then why do I have to listen to you?"
Alden's voice came from behind him.
Alden pointed away from the fire.
He ran back toward the other children.
A moment later Joric shouted from across the clearing that Calist was needed for something extremely important.
It turned out to be a contest involving a sack, a wooden spoon, and rules nobody could agree upon.
He had spent the day carrying tables, tending fires, moving food, watching younger children, and doing work adults once would not have trusted him to do alone.
He still ended the night in the grass arguing with Joric over whether falling outside the marked line counted if someone had been pushed.
Growing older, Calist decided, did not seem to happen all at once.
A few weeks after the harvest feast, Alden mentioned town over supper.
"Garran and I are going in three days."
The first trip returned to him in pieces.
Alden tore a piece of bread in half.
"No. I thought I'd say it to see what your face did."
Alden looked at him as though the answer should have been obvious.

"You're strong enough that taking you makes loading easier. You know how to harness the ox. You know how the wagon needs to be packed. And you've spent the last few months proving I can give you a job without standing over your shoulder until it is finished."
Warmth spread through Calist that had nothing to do with the food.
Calist's hand unconsciously touched the place where his lip had split months earlier.
"If Joric calls them something worse first?"
"Your father believes in training for unlikely disasters."
The second journey to town felt different before the wagon had even left the village.
There was no group of children climbing into the back this time.
Alden went because the smithy needed iron.
Garran went because there was leather to sell and supplies to bring home.
Calist went because his hands made their work easier.
He liked that more than he expected.
Before sunrise he checked the harness with Garran, carried the last sacks to the wagon, and shifted a crate when Alden decided too much weight sat behind the axle.
The morning was colder than on his first journey. A little mist lay in the hollows between harvested fields, and the damp road stayed dark where the rising sun had not yet reached it.
Calist knew the first resting place before the ox began slowing. He knew which wheel Alden would check when they stopped. He knew the rise from which the first town roofs would eventually appear.
When they arrived, he did not stare with his mouth open.
"Disappointing. I was hoping to charge you for it this time."
Calist smiled and lifted the first bundle down.
At Heddan's yard he worked while Alden and Heddan argued over iron.
The new bars were heavier than the things Calist usually carried alone, so Garran took the other end.
Heddan watched them move one stack.
Later, while Alden counted the delivery, Calist checked the ropes.
One bundle sat too close to the edge.
He moved it inward before anyone told him.
Calist had learned that sometimes this meant more than praise.
When the main work was done, Garran handed him a wrapped package.
Alden looked over from the wagon.
There was no warning about getting lost.
No order to stay beside someone else.
They trusted him to cross the market alone and return.
Mira gave him the cloth, a loaf nobody had ordered, and strict instructions that the loaf was for everyone rather than for Joric if Joric happened to intercept him on the road home.
Then he stepped back into the square.
Bram's stall stood near the same edge of the market.
Calist went there without pretending he had another reason.
The dwarf was filing the edge of a narrow metal plate when Calist approached.
His eyes narrowed for a moment.
Then he pointed the file at Calist.
Calist looked down at the work.
"You're filing the edge before joining it."
He thought about the cracked fitting Alden had shown him months earlier.
"Anything trapped between the pieces weakens the join."
"If the surfaces don't meet properly, the heat won't fix that."
Calist looked at the plate again.
"People like blaming heat for bad work. Heat is usually innocent."
"It can when the smith is guilty."
Calist stayed until Bram finished the edge.
Then he remembered the cloth beneath his arm.
"I assumed someone had sent you here for a reason."
"Then go before your father decides dwarves steal children."
Bram looked toward the distant wagon.
He went again the next time the wagon went.
And often enough after that for town to stop being a place Calist only visited in stories.

Sometimes Garran went with another adult. Sometimes the wagon carried more leather than metal. Once it went mostly for salt, lamp oil, grain, and a replacement part for a hand mill that nobody in the village could make properly.
Calist went when the village could spare him and when another strong pair of hands made the journey worthwhile.
There was always something to load.

By then he could harness the ox with only a quick check from whichever adult traveled with him. He knew how much weight could sit behind the axle before the wagon became unpleasant to handle. He knew sacks went where water could not reach them, that leather hated being crushed beneath iron, and that Mira would add something nobody had ordered if she decided the village children looked too thin.
He also knew Heddan complained about prices whether they rose or fell.
And whenever the work allowed it, Calist found Bram.
Bram held up two small hammers.
Calist looked at the piece on the bench.
"I don't want to move much metal."
Calist stared at a tiny clasp.
Finally Calist noticed that one side of the clasp sat slightly higher than the other.
Bram never seemed especially impressed when he knew.
He also never seemed disappointed when he did not.
He simply expected Calist to look again.
That was familiar enough that Calist liked him for it.
The others kept moving along their own paths at the same time.

Eryn spent more mornings with Harlan, Bren, Edrin, or Garran beyond the fields. Short outings became longer ones. She learned when to speak and when silence mattered more. She learned to clean what they brought home and to read signs Calist still saw only as marks in mud.
One afternoon she returned talking about a bear.
They had seen it safely across a broken stretch of woodland and had been quite content to leave it there.
"Big enough that Harlan decided we had somewhere else to be."
"It had a scar across its snout. A huge one. Crooked, like this."
Nalia had been sitting nearby with a scrap of wood in her hands.
Calist forgot the question before supper.
Several days later he found her behind her family's house with wood shavings around her feet.
Nalia immediately turned the object away.
It was supposed to be a bear.
Calist knew this only because Eryn had told the story.
The body was too narrow. One front leg was shorter than the other. The head looked vaguely like a dog that had been insulted.
A deep crooked line crossed its snout.
Calist took the little figure carefully.
The surface smelled fresh where Nalia had cut into it.
She took the bear back and scraped a little more from one shoulder.
"I saw those carved animals in the market."
Nalia looked down at the ugly little bear.
That answer came much faster than the others.

Winter narrowed the number of town journeys. Frost whitened the fields on clear mornings; on milder days rain turned the road heavy and brown, and darkness arrived before the day's work felt finished. It did not end the changes.
Tarin became such a regular part of Mara's work that people sometimes came to the Griffith house asking for him when Mara was elsewhere.

Joric remained impossible to place into one trade. He was good with animals, increasingly useful in the fields, and willing to do almost anything that needed another pair of hands. Nobody seemed especially worried that he had failed to choose one thing.

Nalia's first attempts at sewing with Tessa proved competent enough to be useful and dull enough that she complained about them afterward. Wood was different. She kept finding reasons to work with it.
Calist kept making practical things for Alden and finer mistakes whenever Bram gave him the chance.
By the time the roads became easy again the following spring, Calist was fifteen, and Bram had begun keeping small scraps aside.
A rough ring that needed filing smooth.
A piece of wire that had to be straightened without thinning it.
Things that did not matter much if Calist ruined them.
Which, Calist understood, was exactly why Bram let him touch them.
On one visit Bram pushed a small pair of pliers across the bench.
Calist looked at the open copper ring.
The ring was tiny compared with almost everything Alden had ever asked him to make.
Bram took another ring from a small dish.
On the fourth ring, the ends met without one riding over the other.
Bram took it, turned it between thick fingers, and put it into another dish.
"Then stop standing like a dog waiting for meat."
Outside the stall, the market continued around them.
Someone shouted over the price of onions.
A cart wheel struck a stone.
A child laughed somewhere near Mira's bakery.
Calist bent over the little piece of copper.
For the first time, Bram did not explain what to do.

blocks.alt: Watercolor view of a quiet night forest camp with a small fire, bedrolls, packs, and practical hunting gear.

blocks.text: Harlan arrived at the smithy while Alden was fitting a new handle to a hammer.
Calist looked up from the hinge he was filing.
Harlan rested one hand against the doorframe.
"Ress is still laid up from the boar. Bren and Edrin are coming. Eryn too. I need another pair of hands that can carry without complaining every ten steps."
"Can you carry without complaining every ten steps?"
"And if he says stay where you are—"
The pack felt reasonable when Calist lifted it in the yard.
It felt less reasonable half an hour later.
Harlan walked ahead with Bren. Edrin followed several paces behind them, his bow already unstrung across his back for the first part of the walk.
Eryn moved more easily than Calist despite carrying her own gear.
That irritated him enough to stop shifting the pack.
The village disappeared behind them before sunrise had fully reached the fields.
The old woods looked different when entered with hunters.

Calist had walked beneath those trees many times. He knew the paths nearest the village, the places where children gathered mushrooms, the streambeds, the fallen trunks, and several clearings where the light reached the ground.
Harlan ignored most of those paths.
He moved where the deer moved.
Sometimes that meant a faint track through fern and brush that Calist would never have called a path at all.
Sometimes it meant stopping for no reason Calist could see.
The first time, Calist almost walked into Eryn.
She had stopped because Harlan had raised two fingers.
At first there was only wind moving high in the leaves.
Then a small tapping somewhere ahead.
Farther away, something heavier moved through brush.
By midmorning Calist had learned that hunting involved far more standing still than he had expected.
He had also learned that Eryn could read signs he barely noticed.
She crouched near a patch of soft ground and touched the edge of a print.
Near midday they found fresher sign.
Harlan changed their direction without explanation.
Ahead, between young trees, something moved.
Calist's first instinct was to look at Eryn.
Her bow was already in her hand.
Harlan did not signal her to draw.
Calist could hear his own breathing.
A fly landed on the side of his neck.
He wanted very badly to slap it.
The deer stared toward them for several seconds.
Harlan remained still until the sound was gone.
Only then did he look back.
They made camp late in the afternoon near a shallow rise where the ground stayed dry.
Only a broad patch between trees, a small fire, bedrolls, packs, and a low place where Bren set the cookpot.
Calist spent the next hour doing exactly the sort of things Harlan had brought him to do.
Helping Edrin hang food high enough that animals would have difficulty reaching it.
Clearing stones from where they would sleep.
He discovered that camp work was ordinary work with worse furniture.
Eryn came back with an armful of branches and dropped them beside his pile.
Calist picked up one of hers.
Bren looked over from the fire.
"If the two of you are finished judging sticks, we need more kindling."
"Calist. Dry stuff. Stay where you can see the fire."
"Stay where I can see the fire."
Calist took the small collecting bundle and walked away from camp.
At first he could see the fire easily.
He bent to gather dry twigs beneath a fallen tree.
Then he looked deeper into the woods.
It had been there all day.
It was almost always there now, quiet enough to ignore while people talked or work demanded his hands.
Out here, with the light falling and the voices behind him softer, it became easier to notice.
Not stronger because he was closer.
Just harder to cover with anything else.
Something about the direction ahead felt familiar.
He knew the woods were not safe.
As though he had walked that way before.
As though someone had shown him the path long ago and he had forgotten everything except the feeling of following it.
The bundle remained in one hand.
A low branch brushed his shoulder.
There was no moment when Calist decided to leave the fire behind.
The warm light between the trunks became smaller.
The bundle of kindling lay several paces behind him where he had apparently dropped it.
For one confused second, Calist simply stood there.
Something cooked too close to flame.
Ahead, through brush, a small orange glow moved between trunks.
The other had something hanging from one shoulder that might have been a sack or a rolled hide.
Calist saw its hand begin to move.
An arm clamped across his chest.
Eryn's voice was almost against his ear.
Behind her, Harlan crouched near a tree with Bren farther to the left. Edrin had an arrow nocked.
The arrow struck the ground hard in front of it.
Harlan stood just enough to be seen.
"Dark soon. We don't know how many more are with them. We don't know the ground. We have a camp behind us and one idiot already missing from it."
Bren looked toward the place where the goblins had vanished.
The scolding did not begin until they were back at camp.
Harlan waited until Calist had put down the recovered bundle of sticks.
Then he stood in front of him.
"You carried what you were given. You listened. You kept quiet when it mattered. I sent you for kindling
because I trusted you to manage that without someone holding your hand."
The words hit harder than shouting would have.
"Four people left camp to find you."
"We found your sticks before we found you."
Eryn stood near the fire with her arms folded.
"Or been taken," she continued. "There were tracks going away and no answer when we called."
"If those goblins had found you first, you might be dead. If they'd followed you back, you might have brought them straight to camp."
Calist rubbed one hand over the other.
Calist looked toward the dark trees.
He had explained pieces of it before.
"It feels like somewhere I'm supposed to be."
"When I'm away from the village, sometimes it feels like being pulled home."
"And you never thought this was something people around you should know?"
"Mara knows I wander sometimes. Alden too."
"Do they know you can walk far enough that you don't notice leaving a fire behind?"
"Next time you feel it, you tell someone."
Then he pointed at the edge of camp.
"You wanted to spend the evening wandering through dark trees. Now you can sit still and look at them."
"Anything you see, hear, smell, or merely dislike, you wake me. Two hours."
Calist sat with his back against a log near the edge of camp.
The fire was low behind him.
He held Harlan's spare short spear across his knees, though Harlan had made it very clear that Calist was to wake him rather than attempt anything heroic with it.
For the first half hour Calist heard danger in everything.
Something small scratching near a root.
Calist did not move toward it.
Eryn sat down at his side.
"You should try not walking into goblins."
For a while they sat without speaking.
Then Eryn said, "I can take over."
"Harlan doesn't care who looks at the trees."
"I made everyone come looking. I can sit here for two hours."
A little later she asked, "Is it there now?"
"It's there most of the time now."
"In town it feels like being called home. At first I thought that's what it was."
Calist looked deeper into the forest.
Then she said, "I thought you were dead."
Her voice had lost its teasing completely.
"You weren't answering. Harlan found the tracks and we followed them. I kept thinking we'd find you on the ground somewhere."
Calist tightened his hands around the spear.
"What if one day we don't find you?"
"I don't want to lose you because you followed something you don't understand."
Calist felt heat rise into his face despite the cold night air.
He searched for anything else to say.
She let out a breath that might have been annoyance.
"Once. Farther away. With Bren and Garran."
"One that we saw. Tracks more often."
"Not enough that people talk about it every week."
She rested her hands on her knees.
"The soldiers make them sound like they attack anyone they see."
"Soldiers also tell stories about falling into ditches."
"They steal things sometimes. Traps. Food. Tools if they can carry them. Livestock."
"Then we could tell him later if we were alive."
"Knowing when someone else gets to make the decision is part of being useful."
Harlan appeared with a blanket over his shoulders.
He held out one hand to Calist.
As Calist passed, Harlan added, "You managed not to disappear."
The pull followed him into sleep.
The next morning Harlan sent Calist for water.
He noticed the difference in how the others watched him.
By midday the awkwardness had faded into work.
They found deer sign farther south.
Eryn showed Calist where a branch had been rubbed smooth.
This time he actually saw the difference in the prints before she pointed it out.
Later they took a young buck.
He did not enjoy all of it.
That was not the same as being unable to do it.
He carried more weight on the return journey than he had on the way out.
This time Eryn did not ask whether he was complaining.
She knew he was too tired to answer.
Harlan spoke to Alden before Calist had properly put down his pack.
Two goblins in the woods did not become a village alarm.
It became a place to remember.
A reason not to assume old tracks meant nothing.
Before Eryn left, she caught Calist near the side of the smithy.
She held his gaze for another moment.
At supper, Mara was quieter than Harlan had been.
Calist had almost finished eating when she said, "You disappeared."
"At dusk," she continued. "Without telling anyone. And you found goblins."
Calist looked down at his bowl.
Calist rubbed his thumb against the edge of the table.
Calist tried to explain it again.
The fact that arriving in the village did not make it stop.
When he finished, she asked, "Does it feel dangerous?"
He looked toward the dark window.
"Whatever it is. It feels like I should know."
"When I'm away, it feels like being called home. But when I'm here, it's still there. Past the house. Past the smithy. Toward the woods."
Mara's fingers tightened around her cup.
"And sometimes you can walk without noticing?"
Then Calist asked, "Are goblins always like that?"
Alden tore a piece of bread.
"Most creatures avoid a fight they don't need. Goblins included. Humans are dangerous to them too."
"Because a goat is food. A knife is useful. Cloth is useful. A trap already has work in it."
Mara added, "Being frightened of people does not make hunger disappear."
Calist thought about the two figures between the trees.

"Two goblins you see can be two goblins. Or they can be the front of ten more you don't. It was nearly dark. He didn't know the ground ahead. He had a camp and people behind him. Chasing them would have risked more than it gained."
"So two sightings aren't a big problem."
"They're a reason to pay attention. Not panic."
Alden looked at him for a moment.
"The goblins aren't the part I'm most worried about."
"I can teach you what to do if you see goblins. Harlan can teach you better. None of us can help with a danger you hide from us."
"You didn't tell us how strong it was getting."
Mara reached across the table and touched his wrist.
For several weeks Calist avoided the deeper woods.
That did not stop his feet from occasionally choosing the wrong direction.
Once, carrying a repaired latch toward Joric's house, Calist looked up and found Garran standing beside the road.
The latch was still in his hand.
He had passed the turn toward Joric and was walking toward the old forest.
Another time Eryn caught his sleeve while they were carrying rope from one field to another.
They had drifted off the path.
"What does it feel like right now?"
She let go of his sleeve slowly.
Calist could not argue with that.
He began telling people when he deliberately went walking near the woods.
Most of the time that was enough.
Sometimes the pull still took him farther before Harlan's voice, Eryn's question, or the memory of four people following abandoned sticks brought him back to himself.
And when Calist went to town again, the pull went with him.
At first it felt almost exactly like homesickness.
Then, after the wagon brought him back past the familiar fields and roofs, he understood the difference.
Calist carried that knowledge with him the next time he stood at Bram's bench.
The dwarf placed a tiny copper ring in front of him.
This time the circle stayed a circle.

blocks.alt: Watercolor view of a fine-metalwork workshop filled with small tools, chains, clasps, pendants, and careful bench work.

blocks.text: The next ring closed cleanly too.
Bram turned it between his fingers.
Town visits had settled into a rhythm by then.
He worked for Alden at home. He helped with the wagon when the village needed supplies. He found Bram whenever the work in town left enough time.
Bram stopped treating those visits as interruptions.
A small place appeared for Calist's tools at one end of the bench.
A shallow dish for pieces Calist was not supposed to lose.
The first time Calist put something in the wrong place, Bram moved it without comment.
The second time he said, "If I have to look for your tools, they become my tools."
Calist never misplaced that file again.
The work became smaller as Calist became better.
At Alden's forge, more skill had meant heavier responsibility. Hinges. Tool heads. Fittings. Repairs that had to survive actual use.
At Bram's bench, more skill meant thinner wire and less room for error.
A ring too small to notice from across the room could still be wrong.
A clasp could function and still sit crooked.
A chain could hold and still feel rough against the skin.
"Strong is not the same as good," Bram said one afternoon.
Calist looked at the clasp in his hand.
"Congratulations. You have made a very durable ugly thing."
Bram took it from him and laid it beside another clasp.
The difference was obvious once they were together.
Calist's sat a little high on one side.
"I liked you better when I only visited."
"You still visit. You simply ruin more metal while doing it."
Bram was repairing the setting on a silver brooch when he said, "You keep coming back."
"And you ruin fewer things than you used to."
"If you want to learn this properly, stay."
The market continued beyond the stall.
Someone called out the price of onions.
Calist heard all of it without understanding any of it for several seconds.
"If I meant as a chair, I would have asked you to sit down."
Calist thought about it all the way home.
The village appeared after the familiar bend in the road.
The smithy roof came into view.
The old woods beyond the fields.
The pull was there as it had been in town.
The village still felt like home.
The pull still continued past it.
Calist climbed down from the wagon and unloaded before saying anything.
He carried iron into the smithy.
Stacked it where Alden wanted it.
Helped Garran move a crate toward the storehouse.
Only after the ox had been unharnessed did he find Alden alone.
"Bram offered to take me as an apprentice."
Alden looked at Calist for several seconds.
The answer came so quickly that Calist felt guilty immediately afterward.
"Can Bram teach you things I can't?"
Calist hesitated only because saying it felt wrong.
"You asked me for serious teaching because you wanted to become better. I would be a poor teacher if I kept you from someone who knows what I don't."
"You come back when the village needs you. Harvest. Winter if the roads turn bad. Other times if we ask."
"And when you are here, you work here."
How much work did Bram expect before breakfast?
Had Calist actually seen the bed or merely accepted Bram's claim that one existed?
The rest he promised to ask.
Mara did not tell him no.
That mattered more than the questions.
Two weeks later Calist packed clothing, tools, and enough food for the road.
He left with the village wagon expecting to return for harvest.
Bram's apprentice slept above the workshop.
Calist discovered that on his first evening.
He also discovered that the stairs creaked, the window stuck in damp weather, and the bed was narrow enough that his feet nearly reached the end.
Calist decided this made the room excellent.
His first morning as a proper apprentice began with sweeping.
He stood in the workshop holding a broom.
By midday he had touched almost no hot metal.
"I thought I came here to learn fine work."
"Clean work begins with clean tools, clean metal, and a bench where you can find what you need. If that disappoints you, the door remains where it was yesterday."
Then picked up the cloth again.
The town taught Calist things Bram did not intend to teach.
How early bread arrived at the market.
Which streets flooded after heavy rain.
Where to buy a bowl of stew cheaply near closing time.
Which merchants would wait for payment until a repair was sold and which wanted every copper first.
How loud a town could remain after the village would already have been asleep.
People came to Bram with objects Calist had rarely seen at home.
Decorative buckles from people with enough money to care whether a buckle was decorative.
A silver cup whose owner cared more about a shallow dent than any farmer cared about a scarred shovel.
At first Calist found that ridiculous.
"They pay for what matters to them."
"So does a shirt with one sleeve. Wear one tomorrow."
Calist learned not to make that argument again.
Fine work had its own honesty.
If someone paid for a straight line, the line should be straight.
If a clasp was meant to disappear into the design, it should not announce itself because the smith had been impatient.
If both sides were supposed to match, almost matching was wrong.
The town became full of crooked hinges, uneven handles, badly set rivets, and chains whose links had been closed by people Bram would have insulted for an hour.
When Calist returned home for harvest, he found himself looking at Alden's work differently too.
That pleased him more than he expected.
Alden caught him inspecting a strap fitting.
The first harvest return felt shorter than it was.
There was too much work for anyone to spend long greeting him.
Joric demanded to know whether Calist had become rich.
Nalia asked whether Bram had any broken wooden boxes she could have.
Tarin wanted to know whether town healers used anything Mara did not.
"Some of yours are from being stupid."
Then Garran called them to move grain sacks and the conversation ended.
Several evenings later, after most of the work was done, Calist found Eryn sitting on the low fence behind Garran's house.
For a while neither said anything.
The fields beyond the houses had been cut low.
Smoke from the feast preparations drifted faintly above the village.
"Bram talks enough for both of us."
"You complain about him in every second sentence. I know enough."
"Bram is better at different metalwork. That's not the same thing."
Then she said, "Does he still sell that necklace?"
"The one from the first time. Leaf and arrow."
Calist tried to look as though the question meant nothing.
The words came out before he could stop them.
"One of the reasons I wanted Bram to teach me was—"
Calist felt his face growing hot.
Calist immediately knew this had been the worst possible escape.
"You went to Bram because of reading?"
"Not because of it. He makes me do it."
Calist rubbed both hands over his face.
That finally made her stop enough to listen.
"Mine are. One leaned so far Bram asked whether it was tired."
"My writing looks like the letters are trying to escape."
"Nessa taught me some. Harlan marks things. Garran keeps simple lists."
Eryn considered that far too seriously.
She bumped his shoulder with hers.
Calist stared at the cut field.
Calist nearly returned to the sentence he had abandoned.
Instead he said, "Maybe by next harvest I'll be able to write properly."
"Then you can send me a letter."
Calist spent the walk back deciding which was worse: writing Eryn a letter or telling her why he had wanted to learn fine metalwork.
Bram discovered Calist's lack of reading by accident.
It happened several weeks into the apprenticeship.
He handed Calist a folded piece of paper.
There were several lines of writing.
He recognized something that might have been silver.
The rest became a row of hostile marks.
Calist looked at the paper again.
Bram lowered the file in his hand.
That made Calist like him more than he wanted to admit.
"Alden works in a village where someone walks into his forge and says, 'My hinge is broken.'"
"The letters will not improve overnight out of pity."
Bram used the things already around them.
Calist learned the words he needed because he saw them attached to real things.
Wrote words the way they sounded and then became annoyed when Bram told him that sound had apparently not been consulted when the language was invented.
Bram corrected him without treating the difficulty as a joke.
When Calist truly did not understand, Bram waited.
When Calist was merely careless, Bram made him do it again.
By winter Calist could read simple orders without asking for every second word.
That became useful when he finally attempted the letter to Eryn.
He sat upstairs with a piece of paper for nearly an hour.
Bram came up the stairs, saw the paper, and stopped.
Calist covered it with one hand.
"I know my apprentice has spent an hour writing twelve words."
He told Eryn the market had been crowded.
That Bram had made him remake the same clasp four times.
That he had learned to spell silver and disliked the word.
That he hoped the harvest stores were holding.
He read it three times before sending it with a wagon heading toward the village.
Eryn's reply came two weeks later.
She wrote that deer were moving farther north.
That Nalia had carved another bear and this one now looked like a bear.
That Joric had fallen off a fence while insisting he knew how to repair it.
That Mara wanted to know whether Bram was feeding him.
At the bottom Eryn had added:
Months became seasons through work rather than announcements.
Calist learned to draw wire evenly.
To close chain links without crushing them.
To make clasps that did not catch hair or cloth.
To polish without rounding away detail.
To solder pieces so the join belonged to the object rather than merely holding it together.
He learned that a design drawn on paper could lie.
A line that looked elegant could become weak in metal.
A delicate loop could be too delicate to survive use.
A chain could look balanced and hang badly.
Bram made him sketch before certain jobs.
Calist hated that almost as much as writing.
"Then draw what you intend to make."
"Because your hands should not be the first part of you to discover you have no plan."
Each time the village looked almost the same from the road.
Each time the people inside it had changed a little.
Nalia's carvings became recognizable without explanation.
Tarin began preparing simple remedies when Mara was busy elsewhere.
Joric could take younger workers into a field and return with both the workers and the work mostly intact.
Eryn stopped describing herself as going with the hunters.
Her letters became less frequent during busy seasons and longer when winter kept people near home.
Sometimes Bram corrected his spelling before Calist could stop him.
Once Bram crossed out silver and wrote it correctly above.
In Calist's second year, Bram placed a blank sheet of paper on the bench.
"Because you can follow a design. I want to know whether you can make one."
"Because if the recipient's opinion matters, your bad decisions become embarrassing."
Calist looked back at the paper.
Bram moved to the other side of the bench.
"Shape. Proportion. Material. Thickness. How it hangs. Where the chain sits. How much metal you need including what you will waste. Clasp too."
Calist stared at the blank page.
He added an arrow across it.
"Why is the arrow stabbing the leaf?"
The leaf became larger and softly curved.
The arrow narrowed and passed behind it instead of through it.
Connected without one destroying the other.
Bram turned the final sketch around.
He had started from the memory of a market necklace years earlier.
What sat on the paper no longer copied it.
Calist touched the arrow with one finger.
The first leaf was too flat.
The second curved badly near one edge.
The third survived long enough for Calist to dislike the arrow.
The arrow's fletching became three different problems before becoming one acceptable shape.
The join between them looked heavy.
Bram rarely interfered before Calist asked.
When Calist finally had both pieces ready, he spent longer cleaning the joining surfaces than he once would have spent making the entire object.
Bram watched from the next bench.
When it cooled, the arrow sat behind the leaf exactly as it had on the paper.
The silver leaf caught light softly.
The narrow arrow remained clean behind it.
The first clasp worked but sat badly.
The third closed with a small clean movement and stayed closed when he pulled the chain.
Bram inspected the finished necklace beneath the workshop lamp.
Finally he turned it over in his hand.
Calist looked down at the necklace.
"I never said who it was for."
"I am short. I am not blind."
Calist felt heat rise to his face.
Calist wrapped the necklace in soft cloth and tied the small pouch closed.
He thought of Eryn standing at the market years ago.
The pouch fit easily in one hand.
Calist left for home at the beginning of winter with the necklace packed safely among his things.
He expected to return to Bram when the roads improved.
"Do not forget how to hold a file."
"Then he will send you back early."
By evening the town had disappeared behind the road.
By the next day the familiar hills returned.
Calist touched the pouch once through his pack.
He had not decided how to give it to Eryn.
He decided he had the whole winter to work that out.

blocks.alt: Watercolor view of a village home and attached smithy under heavy winter snow, with warm light inside.

blocks.text: Alden was coughing when Calist came through the door.
Calist noticed because Alden almost dropped the cup in his hand.
Mara looked up from the table.
"He has been saying that for three days."
"Because it has been cold for three days."
Mara hugged him before he could say anything else.
The small pouch with the necklace went into the chest at the foot of his bed.
He intended to take it out again later.
The first days at home were ordinary winter days.
Snow came overnight, thin enough that the road still showed through it by noon.
Calist worked beside Alden in the smithy.
Eryn came by with two knives from Garran and stayed long enough to ask what Bram had made him ruin lately.
Calist considered telling her about the necklace.
Then Joric came through the doorway carrying a bent shovel head and complaining that the ground had frozen in exactly the wrong place.
By the end of the week Mara had stopped accepting his explanations.
Alden stood in the kitchen wearing his work shirt.
Then a broken strap fitting from Garran.
By evening he had forgotten that the smithy was supposed to be temporary work while Alden rested.
Two days later Alden tried to return.
He lasted less than an hour.
Calist heard the hammer strike wrong.
Just without the weight Alden usually put behind it.
Alden had one hand against the edge of the bench.
He did not come back to the forge the next morning.
Illness moved through the village every winter.
This one stayed in more houses than Mara liked.
Tarin spent most days with her.
Calist saw them crossing the road with baskets of dried plants and jars wrapped in cloth.
One of the youngest children developed a chest sickness that kept Mara awake for two nights.
Alden did not improve as quickly.
When it was gone, he became impatient.
At first everyone asked where Alden was.
Then they asked how he was.
After that they simply brought Calist the work.
Halven came in with a plough fitting one morning.
"Tell him the east field is waiting for him to stop being lazy."
Halven placed the fitting on the bench.
Alden's illness did not make everyone forget who Calist had become.
The stores were good enough at the start of winter.
The harvest had been smaller than the best years, but not disastrous.
Nessa would have complained that someone had used too much salt in one of the crocks.
Tessa said so while opening it.
For a moment everyone at the table smiled.
The road vanished beneath it more often.
People mended what they had instead of waiting for new things.
A cracked bowl was bound with wire if the crack did not leak too badly.
Calist spent more time repairing objects that would once have been replaced.
Bram would have hated some of the work.
"Useful first," he said from the chair beside the hearth one evening.
Calist handed him a repaired buckle.
"Then it's beautiful enough for a winter coat."
Alden's voice was stronger than it had been a week earlier.
He still could not work a full day.
That was enough improvement for now.
Calist wrote to Bram when it became clear he would not return with the first easy road.
The message took him less time than letters once had.
That pleased him until he read what he had written.
Alden is still sick. I need to stay until he is better. I will come back when I can.
The words looked too small for what they meant.
Corvin arrived two days later with a patrol heading toward the fort.
Calist met him beside the road.
"Bram Ordek. Metalworker near the market. Mira knows him if whoever carries it can't find him."
Corvin tucked it into his document case.
Calist almost asked how things were at the fort.
"Nothing you can do about it from here."
Three weeks later a trader brought Bram's answer.
Family first. Bench will still exist.
He folded the note and kept it with Eryn's letters.
Alden returned to the forge before the last snow had left the shaded ground.
Calist did not try to stop him.
By planting time he could work most mornings.
He thought about the room above the workshop.
Then Joric came to the forge and asked for help with a broken plough.
Nalia needed a new edge put on a carving tool.
Mara needed someone to carry a basket to a house near the fields.
Garran needed hooks repaired for meat racks.
Then through the first hay cutting.
Calist noticed because the village wagon made fewer trips between the fields and storage.
Because one bin that was usually filled to the top stopped a hand's width below it.
Because Joric stood inside a grain store and stared at the level before closing the door.
"She would say we're measuring it wrong first."
The stew held more roots and less meat.
Children still ran between the tables.
Someone still knocked over a cup.
Joric still ate enough for Nessa's absence to feel particularly noticeable.
Calist laughed when Tessa told him so.
Game became harder to find that autumn.
At first it was only a subject the hunters argued about.
Harlan thought the deer had shifted north.
Garran thought they had moved deeper into the woods.
Eryn listened to all three and went looking.
She returned after two days with a small deer and an opinion of her own.
Sometimes staying out overnight when they once would have come home.
Calist helped more often with the work after they returned.
Helped carry meat when tired hunters reached the village after dark.
One evening Eryn dropped her pack beside the smithy and leaned against the wall.
"If deer move any farther, we're going to need to ask them for directions."
A new wrap covered part of the grip.
The small metal clasp on her quiver strap was one Calist had made.
Eryn pushed away from the wall.
He thought of the necklace in his chest.
Then Alden called for him from inside the forge.
The next winter began with rain instead of snow.
A wagon carrying salt arrived with one wheel tied together by rope and an axle that sounded as though it wanted to die.
Calist and Alden spent half a day repairing it.
The driver said the road south was worse.
A bridge had washed out on a side route.
Two merchants had turned back rather than risk a flooded crossing.
The salt cost more in town.
That mattered to people outside the village.
Inside the village, the sacks were divided where they were needed and the wagon went on.
Nobody passed coins from one village household to another.
The village kept its own account in work, food, memory, and the expectation that help would return when needed.
Calist had grown up inside that system so completely that town prices still felt like a different language.
Portions at supper became a little smaller.
Mara watched the grain jar more carefully.
Tessa repaired blankets that had already been repaired twice.
Joric began checking animal feed before anyone asked.
Children were told not to waste lamp oil.
They simply stopped being careless with what they had.
The first missing trap did not concern Harlan.
The third came back with the chain cut.
Garran laid it on Alden's bench.
Calist picked up the severed link.
"Tracks nearby. Goblin. Maybe more than one."
Nobody said anything for a moment.
The traps continued farther out anyway.
Food did not come closer merely because danger did.
Orc tracks appeared near the northern path before anyone saw an orc.
Then Corvin when a patrol passed through.
Calist went with them because he had been helping repair a boundary fence nearby.
The print was larger than a human foot and broader through the front.
Harlan pointed toward another faint mark.
"Then we know two orcs walked through here."
"What would you like me to know from a footprint?"
Corvin sent two soldiers along the path.
Alden recovered fully enough that by Calist's eighteenth year most visitors to the forge stopped asking about his health.
He still tired sooner after long days.
Calist pretended not to notice until Alden became unreasonable about it.
Their arguments had become very efficient.
Calist considered this one of the advantages of adulthood.
The harder years did not end with Alden's recovery.
Another harvest came in below the old expectation.
The next was better in one field and worse in another.
The fort patrols passed less often.
Corvin still visited, but sometimes months separated one visit from the next.
When he came, he brought familiar complaints and fewer familiar faces.
Merek was still with him most often.
Oren appeared once after nearly a year away and distributed apples to the village children as though no time had passed.
Calist asked where he had been.
Calist no longer asked what that meant.
He could see it in their equipment.
The organized human threat far away had not vanished simply because Calist's village had its own problems.
The crown sent people where the larger armies were.
The pull toward the old woods remained through all of it.
At seventeen it no longer surprised Calist when he felt it in town, at the edge of a field, beside the forge, or walking the road.
Distance did not matter much anymore.
He could be farther from the forest than he had ever been and still know the direction.
He told people when it sharpened.
Sometimes he stopped working and stood still until the almost-dreaming urge to walk passed.
Sometimes Eryn noticed before he spoke.
She would stay nearby until he looked like himself again.
That did not make it less familiar.
If anything, the years made the familiarity stranger.
The feeling had become stronger without becoming threatening.
Some part of Calist still experienced it like recognition just beyond memory.
That was why it remained dangerous.
Near the end of winter, Calist opened the chest at the foot of his bed while looking for a spare belt.
The small pouch lay beneath a folded shirt.
For a moment he thought about taking it to Eryn that evening.
Then Mara called from downstairs that Garran needed help moving a lame goat.
The necklace remained where it was.

blocks.alt: Watercolor view of an empty porch chair with a draped blanket, a simple bow nearby, and a small silver leaf pendant.

blocks.text: Nessa died in the first week of spring.
Tarin came to the smithy before breakfast.
Calist knew from his face before he spoke.
He had seen Nessa three days earlier.
She had complained that Mara's tea tasted like boiled fence bark.
Mara had told her to drink it anyway.
Nessa had drunk it while complaining the entire time.
Calist had carried firewood inside before he left.
She had told him he stacked it badly.
He had promised to improve before she inspected it again.
Then they closed the forge for the morning.
The village had buried people before.
Calist had attended funerals as a child without understanding why adults became quiet afterward.
Nessa's felt different because she seemed to be everywhere even while no longer being anywhere.
A jar in Mara's workroom labeled in Nessa's old hand.
A way of cutting roots Tarin said she had taught Mara, who had then taught him.
A stew nobody could make without someone saying Nessa would have added something else.
Stories whose beginning had belonged to people now dead longer than Calist had been alive.
At the burial, children stood with adults who had once been children in Nessa's kitchen.
Nobody gave a speech long enough to contain her.
A harvest she had organized during the war.
A winter when she had stretched one crock of preserved fruit through three households.
A time she had chased Garran from her kitchen with a spoon because he had stolen cooling bread.
Tessa said she had seen it.
For the first time that day, people laughed.
Afterward he helped carry Nessa's chair back to the porch.
Tessa stopped him before he moved it inside.
Calist set it where it had always stood.
The blanket remained over one arm.
For several weeks nobody sat there.
Spring work gave grief places to go.
Animals had survived winter and immediately began creating new problems.
Joric discovered that three younger boys could turn a simple fence repair into an argument about ownership of a hammer.
Calist repaired the hammer after one of them dropped it on a stone.
Nalia brought him a carved spoon and asked for a narrow metal cap on the end of the handle.
That had become as ordinary as Alden working the forge or Mara carrying herbs.
She went with Harlan, Bren, Edrin, Garran, or the younger hunters depending on the trip.
Sometimes she led the route because she had found the sign first.
Sometimes a younger hunter came to her with a question.
Calist noticed without anyone telling him that she was no longer being brought along to learn.
She was one of the people others learned from.
The trips grew longer because the game remained farther away.
Three became four when the weather or tracks forced it.
They returned tired and dirty, carrying what they had found.
The village used all of it.
He thought about it more after Nessa died.
Not because Nessa had known about it.
As far as Calist knew, she had not.
He simply became more aware of unfinished things.
One evening Eryn sat on the fence outside the smithy while Calist repaired a buckle from her pack.
"You've had that for years," he said.
"You complain about him enough that I can hear him."
Calist thought of the pouch upstairs.
He could have told her to wait.
Then Garran called her from the road and she left.
He told himself he would bring the necklace the next time she came by.
There was always a next time.
Eryn came for arrowheads two days later.
Calist was helping Alden with a wheel band.
The next evening she ate at the Griffith house because Garran and Tessa were helping Harlan prepare hides.
Calist remembered the necklace only after she had gone home.
A week later they walked part of the old path together to check snares.
The pull toward the deeper woods became noticeable halfway there.
Eryn caught the change in his pace.
The feeling was warm in the strangest way.
After a while Calist turned back toward the path.
Calist thought about the necklace on the walk home.
Then they found one of the snares torn apart and spent the rest of the afternoon following tracks with Harlan.
The thought disappeared beneath work again.
A goat vanished from an outer pen before summer.
A cart driver reported seeing three goblins near the north road.
A patrol found old fire pits where no travelers usually camped.
None of it stopped ordinary work.
It changed how people did it.
Children stopped going beyond the last fields alone.
Garran kept more arrows near the door.
The fort sent patrols when it could.
Sometimes that was often enough to notice.
Corvin arrived after nearly two months away with four soldiers and an exhausted horse.
Calist repaired a broken stirrup strap while Corvin spoke with Harlan and Garran.
Corvin rubbed the bridge of his nose.
Garran looked at the four soldiers.
"I can give you two for a day. Maybe three."
The neighboring war was far away.
Its absence could still be felt in the number of horses outside the smithy.
The hunters ranged farther toward the end of summer.
Five prepared to leave one morning: Harlan, Bren, Eryn, and two younger hunters.

One of the younger men, Renn, had been on several proper hunts but still followed Harlan more than he trusted himself. The other, Kell, was younger still and had never been part of a serious fight beyond chasing animals from a pen.
Calist saw them near Garran's house while carrying a repaired pot hook to Tessa.
Eryn was checking the strap of her quiver.
Calist nodded toward Renn and Kell.
Kell was trying to tighten a pack strap while Renn told him he was doing it wrong.
"I'll come by when we're back. One of my buckles is starting to tear."
She grinned and followed the others down the road.
Calist delivered Tessa's hook and went back to the forge.
They were expected back sometime on the third day.
By the following morning Garran had begun looking toward the road whenever someone passed.
Calist noticed because he had started doing the same.
Near midday, someone shouted from the edge of the village.
Calist came out of the smithy.
Harlan walked on his own, but one arm was pressed tightly against his body. A broken arrow shaft protruded from the blood-darkened sleeve above his elbow.
Beside him, Kell had Renn almost entirely across his shoulders.
Renn dragged one leg behind him.
So were Tarin and several others.
"Arrow," Harlan said, indicating his own arm. "His leg's worse."
Mara looked once at the wound.
She looked from Harlan to the road behind him.
"There were too many of them. I couldn't use the bow. Renn's leg was gone under him."
He nodded toward the injured young hunter.
"I told her to come with us."
Kell was staring at the ground.
Harlan looked back toward the road.
The word came harder than anything else he had said.
"I had an arrow through my arm. Renn couldn't walk. Kell was carrying half his weight."
He breathed once through his nose.
Harlan did not look at him.
"By the time I could move again, she was gone through the trees."
Calist looked down the empty road.
Harlan tried to return to the woods before his arm had been properly treated.
Mara stopped him at the door.
"You are not going anywhere with that in you."
Other hunters gathered while she worked.
By afternoon Harlan was back on the trail with Garran, Edrin, and several others.
His arm was bound against his chest.
They went again the next morning.
Corvin sent soldiers when word reached the fort.
They found where the fight had happened.
Signs of Bren's stand farther back among the trees.
Rain came before the search was finished.
On the third evening Harlan came back mud-covered and exhausted.
Garran met him before he reached the houses.
The next morning Calist opened the smithy.
He lit the forge, worked the bellows and set the first piece into the coals.
Alden came in while he was sorting tools.
"She'll be opening that door all day."
Alden stood there a moment longer.
Then he took his apron from the wall.
Around midday Mara brought bread and something warm to drink. Calist ate because she put it in his hand.
Later Joric came by for a repaired buckle.
He did not come closer immediately.
Calist reached beneath the bench, found the buckle and held it out.
Joric looked as though he wanted to say something.
The village kept searching for another two days.
Not as many people went after the rain.
Bren's brother joined them on the second morning.
Nobody asked what they had found.
Tessa left Nessa's chair on the porch.
The blanket was still folded over one arm.
Eryn's place at the table remained where it had always been.
Calist saw it when he brought the repaired hinge.
Calist crouched beside the door and changed it without waiting.
The old screws had worked loose from the wood. He filled the worn holes, set the new hinge and checked the door twice.
Calist put the tools back into his bag.
His eyes went toward the wall beside the door.
There had usually been a bow there.
"I'll be at the smithy if anything else breaks."
His injured arm was still bound close to his chest.
Calist sat near the forge repairing a small kitchen knife.
"She went back before I could stop her," Harlan said.
Calist kept his eyes on the knife.
Neither of them spoke for a moment.
"And Kell, who'd barely seen a real fight."
Calist ran the blade across the stone again.
After a while Harlan said, "Bren knew what he was doing."
"She knew why Bren stayed. She knew what going back meant."
The stone remained beneath Calist's fingers.
He ate when food was put in front of him.
People came to the smithy and spoke to him about ordinary things.
A bent nail that someone insisted could still be saved.
Sometimes he heard footsteps outside and looked toward the entrance before remembering.
Sometimes someone laughed on the road and, for half a breath, the sound was close enough.
One afternoon Mara found him standing beside the well with an empty bucket.
Mara did not ask about what.
She waited until he had filled it, then walked back with him.
A few evenings later Calist went upstairs to change his shirt.
He opened the chest at the foot of his bed and moved a folded tunic aside.
The small cloth pouch lay underneath.
For a while he did not touch it.
He knew exactly what was inside.
The knot came loose beneath his fingers.
The chain he had made one link at a time.
He remembered Bram holding the pendant beneath the workshop light.
He remembered Eryn at the market years earlier, holding another necklace between her fingers.
He remembered thinking that someday he could make one himself.
He had nearly given it to her after supper.
He had thought about taking it to her the next morning.
There had always been another time.
His fingers tightened around the silver.
He bent forward, pressing his free hand against his mouth.
She would never turn it over and find the small flaws he had never quite managed to polish away.
She would never tease him about taking so long.
She would never know why he had started learning work like this in the first place.
He tried to draw another breath.
The necklace trembled in his hand.
Footsteps moved quickly through the house.
Alden's eyes dropped to the silver in his hand.
He sat beside Calist and pulled him against him.
The next came before he had recovered from it.
He buried his face against Alden's shoulder and cried until breathing became difficult, until his throat hurt, until the hand holding the necklace cramped around it.
One arm stayed around Calist's shoulders.
The other rested against the back of his head.
