blocks.text: The forge was busy again by spring.
Alden worked most days beside Calist now. He still tired sooner than he once had, but no longer needed a chair waiting nearby, and Mara had stopped watching him every time he crossed the yard.
She had not stopped watching him entirely.
A broken wheel rim occupied most of the morning.
Alden held it steady while Calist worked the damaged section.
Calist moved it away from the fire.
"Bram would say the heat is innocent."
Outside, Joric was arguing with one of the younger boys about a cart.
A moment later something wooden struck the ground.
The hunters no longer went out alone.
Harlan had made that rule after his arm healed.
There were fewer experienced hunters to argue.
Edrin took more of the longer trips now. Harlan still went whenever his shoulder allowed it. The younger hunters who had once followed mostly to learn began carrying more of the work themselves.
Calist went when the forge could spare him, though nobody pretended he had become a hunter.
He could recognize enough tracks not to embarrass himself.
One morning they found a goat missing from an outer pen.
The fence had been cut rather than broken.
Harlan touched one of the marks in the mud.
That evening, half the village helped.
Weak sections of fence were reinforced.
Animals farther from the houses were brought inward.
Children carried rope and complained about being given the light things.
Joric told them they could carry the heavy things when they stopped dropping the light ones.
One of them immediately dropped a coil of rope.
"You dropped things when you were little."
"He once fell into clean straw while fighting it."
The children forgot their annoyance and demanded the story.
By the time the last animals were moved, half the younger children believed Calist had lost a heroic battle against an entire barn.
Calist decided this was how Nessa must have felt whenever someone remembered a story incorrectly.
Not as sharply as it once had.
Calist tied the final section of rope and went home.
Eryn's absence had become part of the village.
Tessa eventually folded the blanket and took it inside.
Harlan still paused when someone mentioned the eastern ridge.
Bren's name came up whenever one of the younger hunters did something he had taught them.
People laughed at stories about both of them.
The first time that happened, he felt guilty afterward.
Then angry at himself for feeling guilty.
Eryn had laughed more than anyone he knew.
It would have been a poor way to remember her by never doing it again.
So he stopped punishing himself for that.
The necklace remained in his chest.
He had wrapped it again after the day Alden held him.
He had not opened the pouch since.
When he did, there were usually fewer soldiers with him than Calist remembered from childhood.
One afternoon he arrived with Merek and a young soldier Calist did not know.
Calist took the reins while Corvin dismounted.
"How many are left at the fort?"
Corvin handed him a damaged sword belt.
"It means I need this fixed before tomorrow."
Calist led the horses toward water.
Mara fed them until the young soldier looked slightly frightened by the amount still appearing on the table.
Mara put another piece of bread beside him.
Conversation moved between the fort, the road and the village.
A supply wagon had been delayed again.
Another patrol had been reassigned west.
Two farms nearer the border had reported missing animals.
A merchant claimed to have seen an orc near the northern road.
Corvin did not know whether the merchant had actually seen one.
"He described it as eight feet tall."
Joric, who had somehow ended up at supper despite not living there, looked interested.
Years earlier he would have asked about the orc.
Now he asked, "How often are you patrolling north?"
"If they had anyone to send back, I would have them."
Corvin tore a piece of bread.
"The neighboring army doesn't stop needing soldiers because we would like more here."
That had stopped making it easier a long time ago.
The next morning Corvin stood beside his horse while Calist tightened the repaired belt.
Corvin looked down at the work.
Alden was sweeping near the forge.
Corvin gave Calist the belt back.
"Then I'll try not to break it until the next visit."
For a moment Calist looked at the plain military coat.
The same kind of equipment that had fascinated him when he was eight.
Just familiar enough that he knew what each piece cost in work.
The soldiers left toward the fort.
Calist watched them go until Alden called from the smithy.
Summer brought more work than the village had hands for.
Calist spent mornings at the forge and afternoons wherever something else needed doing.
He helped Joric repair a drainage channel.
Helped Nalia lift timber into place for a shed.
Went with Harlan and two younger hunters to check old traps farther east.
Helped Tessa replace a warped section of porch rail.
One evening he sat with Tarin outside the Griffith house while both of them cleaned roots Mara had brought back.
"That doesn't make wasting this one better."
Children were playing near the road.
Another had a stick that had somehow become a spear.
A third had declared herself a dragon and refused to explain why the dragon needed a cooking pot on her head.
Calist watched them chase each other around the well.
One of the younger boys stumbled.
He got up immediately and continued running.
A moment later the dragon struck the swordsman with the wooden spoon she had apparently added to her arsenal.
The swordsman complained this was against the rules.
Nobody knew what the rules were.
At harvest, the village filled the open space with tables again.
There was less food than the feasts Calist remembered from childhood.
Nalia had made several wooden bowls that people were actually using.
She watched every person who touched one.
"Checking whether they work after you already know they work."
She looked at one of her bowls.
"That would not be the bowl's fault."
Joric passed carrying an entire bench alone.
Tarin was with Mara, correcting a younger boy who had brought the wrong herb for one of the pots.
Tessa sat with several other adults near the fire.
Garran was repairing a leather strap while talking to Harlan.
Somebody shouted because a cup had been knocked over.
A dog escaped with a piece of meat and immediately became the most important thing in the village.
Calist stood in the middle of it.
People arguing over things that did not matter.
Children being corrected by adults who were not their parents.
Calist looked toward the road leading to the fort.
Alden found him in the smithy after the feast.
Most of the fires outside had burned low.
Calist hung a pair of tongs on the wall.
For several seconds the only sound was the low crackle from the forge.
"You're not doing this because of Eryn."
Calist rested both hands against the edge of the workbench.
Calist looked toward the open doorway.
The last of the feast was being cleared away outside. Someone dragged a bench across the ground. Joric's voice carried from somewhere near the tables.
"I want this to still be here."
Calist gestured vaguely toward the doorway.
"The fields. The houses. People complaining about work. Joric being an idiot."
"I heard that!" came faintly from outside.
"Mara feeding everyone who comes through the door."
He looked down at his hands.
"Nalia making things. Tarin knowing everything before anyone else does. Children fighting with sticks and getting in everyone's way."
"I don't want people here learning to live like every trip into the woods might be the one someone doesn't come back from."
"I don't want moving the animals closer to the houses to become normal because nobody thinks they're safe farther out."
"Corvin can't cover everything with the men he has."
Calist rubbed one thumb against the edge of the bench.
"I can't fix the war in the west. I know that."
"And joining the army doesn't mean they'll put you here."
"You could spend months guarding a storehouse and never see this road."
"But somebody has to do those things too."
Alden was quiet for a long time.
Some tightness he had not noticed until then eased from his shoulders.
"I will not do it for you."
"I spent years wishing someone had given me the choice you have now."
"That means I'm not going to take the choice away from you because I'm afraid of the answer."
Calist remained beside the workbench for a while.
Eventually Mara called that supper was getting cold.
Mara knew before Calist finished the first sentence.
He could tell by her face.
She put down the cloth she had been folding.
Alden stayed very interested in the cup in his hands.
"When Corvin comes through again. Or I can go to the fort."
She lowered her eyes to her hands.
"I want you to take over the forge and complain about your back when you're older than your father."
"I want you to finish with Bram."
He could see a piece of the road in the darkness outside.
"Because I want to come back to those things."
"And I want everyone else to be able to keep doing them while I'm gone."
Calist did not try to fill it.
She came around the table and put both arms around him.
"I don't know what else to say."
Mara pulled back just enough to look at him.
Neither smiled until Mara turned away.
He had five soldiers with him.
Calist was shoeing a horse when they arrived.
Corvin dismounted and watched him finish setting the last nail.
Alden came from behind the forge.
Corvin looked from one to the other.
They waited until the horse was settled.
Corvin studied him for a few moments.
"Fort takes volunteers. I can bring you with us when we leave if you want."
"I don't choose where they post him."
"I can't promise he stays at my fort."
"I can't keep him out of danger."
"But if he does end up with you—"
"That does not mean you get special treatment."
"I'll teach him what I can. I'll correct him when he needs it. If he does something stupid, I'll tell you."
"You realize he'll be an adult soldier, not the boy who followed me around with a broom."
That evening Calist opened the chest at the foot of his bed.
The pouch was where he had left it.
He carried it to the forge.
Alden was inside finishing a set of nails.
He looked at the cloth in Calist's hand.
Then went back to his work.
For a while he only looked at it.
Then he took out the tools Bram had given him.
Tools an apprentice should already possess.
The pendant remained intact in his palm.
He did not want to melt it.
He did not want to make another necklace either.
The back was broad enough for what he had in mind.
He found a narrow piece of silver he had kept from another job and began shaping it.
Alden's hammer stopped for a moment.
The backing had to sit flat.
The pin had to move freely.
The catch had to hold without opening when cloth pulled against it.
The first pin sat too high.
He prepared both surfaces carefully before heating them.
No gap he expected the heat to forgive.
Bram's voice returned from years earlier.
Calist soldered the backing into place.
The leaf and arrow remained on the front.
Smaller now without the chain around them.
The piece no longer looked like something meant to hang against Eryn's chest.
Calist fitted the pin behind it.
His father turned the clasp beneath the lamplight.
Calist ran his thumb once over the silver leaf.
There had been so many times he could have given it to her.
He had believed every one of them would be followed by another.
Calist fastened the clasp to the edge of his cloak.
The next evening Alden brought the wooden chest into the main room.
He had seen it opened throughout his childhood.
Alden knelt and lifted the lid.
The chainmail lay beneath folded cloth.
Leather at the collar and edges, replaced where age had demanded it.
The mail settled heavily in his hands.
"You plan to join soldiers. You may as well discover whether this fits before one of them is laughing at you."
The weight surprised him despite knowing how much mail weighed.
He pulled it over his head.
The rings settled across his shoulders and chest.
The shirt was a little loose in one place and tighter than ideal in another.
Calist had not heard her enter.
Her eyes stayed on the mail for a moment.
Then Alden reached into the chest again.
Nothing on it that would make anyone look twice.
Alden drew it a few inches.
He had done the same thing for as long as Calist could remember.
The weapon felt different from every sword he had handled while helping soldiers at the forge.
The sword Alden had carried because someone had ordered him to war.
Now he was giving it to a son choosing to go.
Alden adjusted one of the mail straps.
The chainmail returned to the chest afterward.
Not because Calist had changed his mind.
He had work in the morning.
There were still several days before Corvin expected to pass through again.
Calist fastened the silver clasp to his cloak and left it there.
At supper, Joric arrived carrying a loaf of bread.
Tarin came through the door a few minutes later because Mara had asked him to bring dried leaves from her workroom.
Alden complained that nobody remembered which house they belonged to.
Outside, evening settled over the village.
A child shouted from farther down the road.
The forge was quiet for the night.
Calist sat at the table between the people who had filled most of his life.
Mara put another bowl in front of Joric before he could ask.
Joric immediately began arguing that he had not been about to ask.
Tarin told him nobody believed him.
Calist smiled and ate with them.
